item.title: Art Tax Border: Italy-Switzerland
item.description: The tax frontier between Italy and Switzerland in the circulation of works of art: VAT on importation, confiscation and proportionality after Court cost. n. 93/2025
item.content:encoded:
Abstract This contribution starts from the Cass order. civ., Sec. Unite, of 25 August 2026, n. 24764, to show how the story relating to the introduction into Italy, from Switzerland, of a work of art of high value constitutes a privileged observatory on the relationships between customs law, VAT on imports and the sanctioning system. The 2026 ordinance, however, does not define the merit of the controversy: after the ruling of the Constitutional Court no. 93/2025 and the self-defence annulment of the confiscation order, the parties renounced the appeal and the judgment was declared extinguished. Precisely this "non-decision", however, allows us to enhance the central issue: despite the high degree of economic integration between Switzerland and the European Union, the circulation of works of art and high-value goods continues to encounter a real **fiscal border** for VAT purposes. The article analyzes the distinction between duties and VAT on imports, the meaning and limits of the EEC-Switzerland Agreement of 22 July 1972, the postponement of the art. 70 d.P.R. n. 633/1972 to customs regulations, the effects of the decriminalization of simple smuggling and, above all, the remodulation of confiscation in light of the principle of constitutional and Euro-unitary proportionality.
Introduction The order of the Cass. civ., Sec. Unite, of 25 August 2026, n. 24764, is a procedurally conclusive but substantially interlocutory provision. It does not resolve the interpretative issue originally referred to the United Sections regarding the survival and operation of customs confiscation in relation to VAT on imports after the decriminalization of simple smuggling; on the contrary, it notes that, in the meantime, the Constitutional Court has affected the regulatory framework with sentence no. 93/2025 and that, following the self-defense cancellation of the confiscation order by the customs administration, the parties renounced the appeal, with the consequent extinction of the proceedings. It is precisely this circumstance that makes the case particularly significant. The story arises from the introduction into Italy, coming from Switzerland, of a painting of enormous value, not declared at customs and with import VAT not paid. It touches on an essential point in Italy-Switzerland relations: the absence or mitigation of duties in trade does not eliminate the relevance of VAT on imports, which continues to mark a clear "tax border line" between Swiss territory and EU territory. The underlying thesis of this contribution is twofold. First of all, the case demonstrates that, even in the context of an intense economic exchange and a consolidated conventional framework between Switzerland and the European Union, a fully operational fiscal border remains for VAT purposes, particularly sensitive for works of art and high-value goods, for which the declarative fulfillment and the correct qualification of the operation take on decisive importance. Secondly, the Constitutional Court ruling. n.
93/2025 can be read as the transition from a substantially automatic confiscation model to a system that is more respectful of the principle of proportionality, especially when the State's fiscal interest has been fully satisfied through payment of the tax, accessories, interest and financial penalty.
The story: from the incident in 2012 to the termination of the judgment in 2026 According to what appears from the documents reported in the 2026 Ordinance of the United Sections, on 3 October 2012 the taxpayer was checked at the Milan-Linate airport while he was introducing a painting of considerable value into Italy from Switzerland, without declaration and without payment of VAT on import, amounting to €448,443.00. At first the criminal proceedings followed; subsequently, as a result of the decriminalization of simple smuggling carried out by Legislative Decree no. 15 January 2016. 8, the criminal trial ended with acquittal because the fact was no longer foreseen by law as a crime, with transmission of the documents to the administrative authority. The customs administration first ordered the seizure and then the confiscation of the property, recalling the articles. 282 and 301 of the TULD in connection with the art. 70 of the Presidential Decree n. 633/1972. The Lombardy CTR believed that the confiscation pursuant to art. 301 TULD had been substantially overwhelmed by decriminalisation, in the absence of express provision of additional sanctions for the resulting administrative offence. The question, due to its systematic importance, was referred to the United Sections first by the Fifth Section with interlocutory order no. 21917/2023 and then, with interlocutory order no. 18284/2024, to the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court, with sentence no. 93/2025, declared the constitutional illegitimacy of the art. 70, first paragraph, Presidential Decree n. 633/1972, in the part in which it does not provide that, in case of application of the art. 301 TULD, the things subject to the violation are not confiscated if the obligor provides for the full payment of the evaded amount, the accessories, the interests and the financial penalty.
At that point, the Customs Agency independently annulled the confiscation order and the parties jointly waived their appeal to cassation; the United Sections, with ordinance no. 24764/2026, therefore declared the termination of the proceedings. A point arises that must be expressly clarified: ordinance no. 24764/2026 does not resolve the merits of the question originally submitted to the United Sections, but closes the process due to the lack of interest in the dispute following the decision of the Council and the administrative self-defense.
The Italy-Switzerland fiscal border: position of Switzerland with respect to the customs and VAT territory of the Union Switzerland belongs neither to the customs territory of the Union nor to the common VAT system of the Union. The introduction of goods from Switzerland into Italian territory constitutes, from the Union and national point of view, an "import", with consequent activation of customs regulations and, as a rule, VAT on import. Legitimacy jurisprudence has repeatedly underlined that the 1972 Agreement abolished or progressively eliminated duties in trade between Switzerland and the Community/Union for the relevant products, but "did not include Switzerland in the customs territory of the Community" nor did it eliminate VAT upon entry of the goods. In this sense, already Cass. pen. n. 32111/2023 reiterates that, although customs smuggling linked to duties cannot be configured in certain cases, the possible evasion of VAT on imports remains distinct, subject to the limit of the prohibition of double taxation. On a systematic level, the Civil Court of Cassation has clarified that VAT on importation constitutes an internal tax, although it shares with duties the genetic moment of importation and some procedural and sanctioning specificities. Ordinance no. 21917/2023 in fact highlights that VAT on imports "is the same tax as intra-union VAT", although subject, as a result of art. 70 d.P.R. n. 633/1972, to the sanctioning provisions specific to border rights.
This approach allows us to grasp the core of the cross-border profiles: a full customs border does not operate between Switzerland and Italy in the same terms as relations with any third country unrelated to preferential agreements, but a "VAT fiscal border" still remains. For works of art and high-value goods, this means that the physical passage of the good across the border can determine, except for specific suspensive or temporary regimes, the onset of the VAT obligation and related declaration obligations.
Customs duties and VAT on imports: structural distinction and application consequences One of the major practical misunderstandings in the circulation of works of art between Switzerland and Italy consists in assuming that the absence of duties is equivalent to the absence of import tax. The sources examined by the writer clearly deny this automatism. The Supreme Court recalled that the Court of Justice expressly stated that import duties do not include VAT to be collected for the importation of goods. At the same time, national jurisprudence notes that VAT on imports originates from the fact of importation into the Union and subsequent introduction into the economic circuit of the Member States, but remains distinct from duties, although linked to them in terms of operative event and chargeability. Administrative practice also confirms that, for imported goods, the tax generating event occurs at the time of importation and, when the goods are subject to customs duties, the chargeability of VAT is coordinated with that of duties; this does not mean, however, that the VAT debt depends on the existence of a duty due. This is the decisive point in relations with Switzerland: the preferential agreement can eliminate the duty, but not the VAT. Hence the practical importance of the distinction. A collector or operator may find themselves in a situation where: - no duty is due by virtue of the conventional regime or the origin of the goods; - but VAT on importation is still due in Italy, as it is an internal tax collected upon entry of the goods into the territory of the Union.
The absence of this awareness is particularly risky in the art market, where the value of the asset is often very high and where personal transport, specialized shipping or circulation for exhibitions and restorations can lead to underestimating the tax figure.
The EEC-Switzerland Agreement of 22 July 1972: relevance and limits The Agreement between the European Economic Community and the Swiss Confederation of 22 July 1972, concluded with EEC regulation no. 2840/72, has been constantly evoked in the litigation as a parameter for evaluating the import regime from Switzerland. It provides for the gradual elimination of customs duties on imports in trade between the parties, the prohibition on introducing new duties and new taxes with equivalent effect, as well as a regulation inspired by the principle of "commercial neutrality". However, the Court of Cassation has repeatedly ruled out that the agreement prevents the collection of VAT upon entry of goods into Italian territory. In particular, it was stated that VAT on imports has a different financial basis from customs duties, does not constitute a duplication of them, and continues to be due to the State at the time of entry of the goods, unless it is proven that the tax has already been paid previously, with the exclusion of discriminatory double taxation. For the topic considered here, the 1972 agreement therefore performs an ambivalent function: on the one hand, it reduces or breaks down the tariff barrier, favoring trade; on the other hand it does not eliminate the VAT barrier, which remains autonomous. The systematic consequence is that the intense economic relationship between Switzerland and Italy does not translate into full fiscal assimilation. Compared to the EU VAT system, Switzerland remains an external system; therefore, the entry of the good into Italy continues to be, in principle, an event qualified for tax purposes as an import. Art. 70 Presidential Decree n. 633/1972 and customs regulations: the reference to articles. 282 and 301 TULD
The art. 70 d.P.R. n. 633/1972 constitutes the cornerstone of the connection between VAT on imports and customs regulations. The provision establishes that the tax relating to imports is assessed, liquidated and collected for each operation and adds that, for disputes and sanctions, the provisions of the customs laws relating to border duties apply. This postponement has historically allowed the extension to VAT on imports of sanctioning institutions typical of customs law, including the confiscation provided for by the art. 301 TULD in connection with the smuggling hypotheses referred to in the art. 282 TULD. Interlocutory ordinance no. 21917/2023 precisely reconstructs the point: art. 70 recalls the sanctions provided for by customs laws on border rights, also including confiscation, understood in a broad sense as an ablative measure linked to the evasion of VAT on imports. Here a dogmatic knot of great importance emerges. On the one hand, import VAT is qualified as an internal tax and structurally homogeneous with internal VAT; on the other hand, for historical and functional reasons, its procedural and sanctioning regulations are based on customs law rules. This is a regulatory hybridization that explains many of the tensions that have resulted in the question of constitutional legitimacy. On a ratione temporis level, for the events of 2012 the reference discipline was that of the TULD referred to in the art. 70 in the text then in force. Subsequent regulatory developments, including those enhanced by the jurisprudence of 2024-2026, cannot therefore be mechanically back-projected onto the original facts, but are relevant for understanding the change in the interpretative and constitutional framework.
Decriminalization of simple smuggling and the problem of the survival of confiscation Legislative Decree no. 8/2016 decriminalized simple smuggling, opening up the problem of the fate of accessory measures and, in particular, of confiscation in cases of failure to pay VAT upon importation. The question was whether, once the crime no longer existed, the mandatory confiscation of the property subject to the violation could survive in the administrative context. The United Sections, in interlocutory order no. 18284/2024, record the contrast. On the one hand, the administration supported the persistent administrative applicability of mandatory confiscation; on the other, the taxpayer invoked the principle of legality and the unreasonableness of a system that would have retained a very severe ablative measure after decriminalization. Ordinance no. 21917/2023 underlines the particular affliction of customs confiscation pursuant to art. 301 TULD, broader than ordinary confiscation pursuant to art. 240 of the Criminal Code, and recalls its traditional qualification as a safety measure based on the dangerousness of the thing, not on the dangerousness of the subject. But this very framework proved insufficient to neutralize the doubts of proportionality, especially when the confiscation was accompanied by already very high financial penalties and when the debtor had fully satisfied the tax demand. The cross-border case with Switzerland has made the problem even more evident: an asset of very high value, such as a work of art, can be confiscated for VAT evasion on import, with financial effects potentially much higher than the tax due, especially in the absence of residual damage for the treasury after full payment.
Nature and function of confiscation: legality, guarantee and proportionality The jurisprudence oscillates between two readings of confiscation. According to one line, it does not have a sanctioning nature in the strict sense, but constitutes a real security measure aimed at avoiding the further use or circulation of illegal goods. According to another perspective, without denying its formal qualification, its concrete cumulation with pecuniary sanctions and its automatic nature impose a proportionality control similar to that required for administrative and tax sanctions. The United Sections of 2024 grasp the problem well: the fixed and automatic nature of the measure ends up affecting overall different facts in the same way, also neglecting the subsequent conduct of the offender, such as the full payment of the evaded tax and the financial penalties. Hence the doubt of compatibility with the art. 3 Constitution and with the art. 49 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. The Constitutional Court, in sentence no. 93/2025, does not fundamentally eliminate confiscation from the VAT system on imports. Rather, it redesigns its legitimate operation, deeming its maintenance disproportionate when the perpetrator of the offense takes action to remedy the non-payment, paying the tax evaded, the accessories, the interests and the financial penalty. In this case, the guarantee function that can justify mandatory confiscation is lost, since the State has already recovered the entire tax debt.
The decision thus lends itself to being read as a transformation of the model: from confiscation as a substantially automatic consequence of the violation, to confiscation as a measure that must be reversed when the fiscal interest has been fully satisfied.
The ordinance of the United Sections n. 18284/2024: the reasons for the referral to the Constitutional Court Interlocutory ordinance no. 18284/2024 represents the true theoretical crux of the story. The United Sections observe, first of all, that in the specific case the taxpayer had already paid in full both the tax evaded and the administrative sanctions imposed before the adoption of the confiscation order. Starting from this data, the Court highlights that the sanctioning structure resulting from the art. 70 d.P.R. n. 633/1972, in relation to the articles. 282 and 301 TULD, appeared difficult to reconcile with the principles of reasonableness and proportionality. The ordinance compares three plans: - the VAT regime on imports; - the internal VAT regime; - the customs duties regime. Compared to internal VAT, confiscation does not operate in similar terms, or in any case it can be reversed upon payment of the tax debt pursuant to art. 12-bis of Legislative Decree no. 74/2000; with respect to duties, the Union Customs Code provides that, in the event of confiscation, the customs debt is extinguished, so that the cumulation of the full tax claim, financial penalty and confiscation of the goods appeared excessive. It is particularly important that the United Sections have excluded the practicability of a constitutionally oriented interpretation of the art. 70, deeming the literal reference to customs sanctions insurmountable and therefore referring the matter to the Council. The case thus shows a paradigmatic example of dialogue between the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Court and Union law on a matter with a strong technical-tax density but with clear implications for the protection of property rights.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). Constitutional Court no. 93/2025: the remodulation of the confiscation Sentence no. 93/2025 of the Constitutional Court constitutes the point of balance reached by the system. The Consulta takes note, in line with EU jurisprudence and legitimacy, of the structural identity between import VAT and internal VAT, despite the different procedural and sanctioning framework of the former. Precisely this identity makes a radically more burdensome sanctioning treatment for import VAT problematic, especially when it involves the automatic ablation of the good even after full compliance. The Court underlines that the principle of proportionality also concerns tax sanctions and is based not only in art. 3 of the Constitution, but also in the EU obligations to which Italy is bound, in particular in the art. 49, par. 3, CDFUE. It specifies that the disproportion found is not "intrinsic" to the confiscation as such, but rather "relative" or "ordinal", in comparison with other sectors of the legal system: the duties regime and the internal VAT regime. The solution adopted is additive: the art. 70 is constitutionally illegitimate in the part in which it does not provide that, in case of application of the art. 301 TULD, the things subject to the violation are not confiscated if the obligor provides for the full payment of the evaded amount, the accessories, the interests and the financial penalty. The systematic effect of the decision is notable. Confiscation remains abstractly compatible with the import VAT system, but its maintenance is no longer justifiable when the purpose of guaranteeing collection has ceased. A model is therefore outlined in which the ablative reaction must give way in the face of full satisfaction of the fiscal interest.
The cross-border implications for the art market between Switzerland and Italy The works of art constitute the ideal terrain for observing the persistent fiscal border between Switzerland and Italy. These are goods: often of very high value; frequently mobile and intended for international circulation; sometimes accompanied by complex documentation or intermediate steps; susceptible to transfer for sale, storage, restoration, exhibition or inheritance. In this context, ordinance no. 24764/2026, although not deciding the merit, retains a strong symbolic and practical importance. Symbolic, because it shows that the system has felt the need to correct, through the Constitutional Court, the excesses of an ablation apparatus designed for traditional customs repression but applied to VAT on imports. Practical, because after sentence no. 93/2025, the position of the operator who has fully paid the amount due is significantly strengthened against the permanence of the confiscation. However, it remains clear that the constitutional decision does not attenuate the substantial obligations of declaration and payment. It does not erase the fiscal frontier; it only makes the sanctioning consequences more proportionate in cases of subsequent full regularization. For the art market, the message is clear: preventive compliance remains essential, but the system can no longer demand, once the tax interest has been fully satisfied, a further and potentially disproportionate financial sacrifice represented by the definitive loss of the asset.
Conclusions The case resulted in Cass. civ., Sec. United, order. n. 24764/2026 demonstrates first of all that the high economic integration between Switzerland and the European Union has not erased the VAT fiscal frontier. Switzerland remains outside the customs territory and the common VAT system of the Union; consequently, the introduction of works of art and high-value goods into Italy continues, as a rule, to integrate a fiscally relevant import. The absence of duties, or their mitigation as a result of the 1972 Agreement, does not imply the absence of VAT on imports, which retains functional and regulatory autonomy. On the sanctioning level, the relationship between art. 70 d.P.R. n. 633/1972 and TULD has for a long time produced a regime of particular severity, culminating in the possibility of confiscation of the property. The decriminalization of simple smuggling brought to light the contradictions of this system, especially when the ablative measure survived in the administrative context even after full payment of the tax and sanctions. Ordinance no. 18284/2024 has correctly transformed this tension into a question of constitutionality; the Constitutional Court ruling. n. 93/2025 responded by imposing a proportionate reading of the confiscation, incompatible with its maintenance once the fiscal interest of the State has been fully satisfied. Finally, perhaps the most interesting fact remains: ordinance no. 24764/2026 is not the final decision on the merits that one might have expected, but the procedural registration of a solution that has now developed elsewhere - in constitutional jurisprudence and administrative self-defense.
In this sense, the "non-decision" of the United Sections confirms the relevance of the case: not for what it formally decides, but for what it allows us to understand about the persistent fiscal specialty of the Italy-Switzerland border and the need, no longer avoidable today, to also subject the customs confiscation applied to VAT on importation to the scrutiny of the principle of proportionality.

item.title: Living in Mornago, working in Ticino: taxation and permit G
item.description: From 1 January 2024, the New Frontier Agreement guarantees a €10,000 exemption to new frontier workers. Discover taxation, AVS, LPP and LAMal for those who live in Mornago and work in Ticino.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Withholding tax only in Switzerland, no double taxation - Exemption €10,000 per year (new cross-border workers), transitional regime until 2033 - AVS and LAMal mandatory; LPP from 7-18% depending on age group - Permit G allows unrestricted access to the Ticino labor market
## Key facts - **What**: Working in Ticino while residing in Mornago as a cross-border worker - When: From January 1, 2024 (entry into force of the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020) - Where: Mornago (Varese province, Italy) → Canton Ticino (Switzerland) - Who: Cross-border workers with Permit G and an employment contract - Exemption: €10,000 annually (new cross-border workers from July 17, 2023 onwards) - AVS rate (employee): 5.3% on gross salary
Working in Canton Ticino while living in Mornago is a well-established choice for professionals in the province of Varese. The Italy-Switzerland Double Taxation Convention, signed on December 9, 1976, has eliminated the risk of paying taxes in both countries. For cross-border workers, a specific rule applies: the withholding tax is deducted exclusively by Switzerland, not by Italy. Italy recognizes the tax credit through the CE section of the 730 declaration.
Permit G is the essential document for those living in Mornago and working in Ticino. It is not a temporary visa but a work permit that allows unrestricted access to the Ticino labor market without sectoral restrictions. The application is submitted to the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) with the employment contract signed by the Swiss company and the Italian identity document.
January 1, 2024, marked the entry into force of the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, agreed on December 23, 2020, and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of June 13, 2023. The agreement introduced a clear distinction: cross-border workers already employed as of July 17, 2023, retain the €7,500 annual exemption until 2033 (transitional regime); those starting after that date benefit from a €10,000 exemption. The exemption represents the annual gross income exempt from Italian tax.
The Swiss pay slip includes several elements. The gross salary is immediately subject to AVS (employee rate 5.3%), AI (disability, included in the AVS rate), IPG (unemployment insurance, included), and ADD (ordinary unemployment, 1.1% up to the annual cap of CHF 148,200). In addition to the mandatory contributions, there is the LPP (Professional Pension Fund, second pillar), which varies from 7% to 18% of the pay slip depending on age: a 25-34-year-old employee contributes about 7%, while a 55-64-year-old reaches 18%. The LAINF (accident insurance), managed by SUVA, is paid by the employer with rates ranging from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector of activity.
### The pension framework for the cross-border worker The AVS is not a tax but a social security contribution that generates pension rights. Those working in Switzerland accumulate valid contribution years for the Italian and Swiss pensions thanks to international agreements. The LPP (second pillar), on the other hand, is complementary pension managed by private funds of the company or by pension institutions, and generates a life annuity or a capital upon reaching retirement age.
The benefits for those living in Mornago and working in Ticino also include the possibility of choosing between Swiss health insurance (LAMal) and Italian health insurance (CMI). LAMal covers the entire Swiss territory and guarantees high-level medical services; the deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually depending on the chosen plan. The choice must be made within 3 months of the start of the employment relationship. ### Taxation and withholding tax in Switzerland
The Swiss withholding tax is the basis of the tax system for cross-border commuters. Unlike many European countries, Switzerland deducts taxes directly from the paycheck and transfers them to the cantonal administration. For those living in Mornago and working in Ticino, this means there is no double direct taxation: Italy does not withhold additional national taxes on foreign employment income but recognizes the Swiss tax credit in the income tax return through the CE section of the 730 form or the Redditi PF declaration.
The withholding tax rate varies by canton. The Canton of Ticino applies combined federal and cantonal rates: the federal part is set according to a progressive table (from about 6% to about 13% depending on income), and the cantonal part is added to this. A person earning CHF 50,000 annually will have a total deduction (tax + social contributions) significantly lower than Italian taxation on an equivalent income in euros.
The New Cross-Border Agreement, which came into effect on January 1, 2024, has profoundly changed the tax treatment. For new cross-border commuters (those who started after July 17, 2023), the annual exemption has been increased from €7,500 to €10,000, with a gradual reduction in the transitional period 2024–2033. Cross-border commuters already employed retain their acquired rights: they remain tax-exempt up to €7,500 annually until 2033, after which the exemption drops to €5,000. This structure offers protection for low and medium incomes, typical of the province of Varese.
The withholding tax is administered by the AFC (Federal Tax Administration) at the federal level, while the Canton of Ticino manages the cantonal surcharge through the Cantonal Tax Office. The Swiss employer automatically deducts these amounts and transfers them to the competent authorities; the cross-border commuter does not need to file a separate declaration in Switzerland (except in cases of multiple employments or additional income).
### Mandatory Social Contributions: AVS, LPP, ADD, LAINF
Swiss social contributions are distinct from ordinary taxation and generate pension and protection rights. The AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance, OASI, and Disability Insurance, DI) represents the first pillar and has a dependent rate of 5.3% (the IPG, unemployment gain, is included). The employer pays the corresponding amount, thus creating an overall rate of 10.6%. This is not a tax deduction but a right: each year of Swiss contribution also counts for the Italian pension, thanks to international treaties.
The ADD (unemployment insurance, equal to a rate of 1.1%) covers the cross-border commuter in case of job loss in Switzerland. The contribution ceiling is set at CHF 148,200 annually: those earning more do not pay additional ADD. The AC (natural disaster insurance) is part of the same contribution.
The LPP (Professional Pension Fund, second pillar) is mandatory from the age of 25. The rate varies depending on age: from 25 to 34 years it is approximately 7%, from 35 to 44 approximately 10%, from 45 to 54 approximately 14%, from 55 to 64 approximately 18%. This progressive structure reflects the principle that younger employees contribute less because they have more time to accumulate capital. The LPP is managed by private pension institutions (foundations, insurance companies) and generates a pension or capital upon reaching retirement age (65 years for men, 64 for women in Switzerland, but the Italian cross-border worker retains access to rights also towards the INPS).
The LAINF (insurance against occupational accidents and professional diseases) is managed by SUVA and is financed by the employer with a rate between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity. It covers work accidents, professional diseases, and entails medical benefits, indemnity benefits, and, in case of death, benefits to family members.
### Comparison between Italian and Swiss rates
From a theoretical point of view, an identical gross salary has a very different net amount depending on whether it is received in Switzerland or Italy. The Italian IRPEF has progressive rates: 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, and 43% over €50,000. In Switzerland, the federal withholding tax is lower (6–13% depending on income), and the Canton of Ticino adds an additional cantonal component. Although Switzerland also has AVS/AI/IPG (5.3%) and LPP contributions (7–18%), the total is often lower or comparable to the Italian IRPEF alone on average incomes. For low incomes (below €28,000), the Swiss advantage is even more marked thanks to the exemption of €10,000 (new cross-border workers) or €7,500 (old cross-border workers).
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). # ## Health insurance: LAMal and right of option for G border workers Border workers with G Permit have an explicit right of option on health coverage. They can choose to join the LAMal (Swiss Health Insurance, mandatory for Swiss residents) or stay in the Italian system with the CMI (Maternity-Invalidity-Igiene Coverage). The choice must be communicated in writing within 3 months of the start of the employment relationship. Many border workers opt for LAMal because Ticino health facilities are accessible without geographical barriers, and covered services include general practitioners, hospitalisation, prescription drugs and specialist services throughout Switzerland. LAMal adult deductibles range from CHF 300 (minimum deductible, with higher premium) to CHF 2,500 (maximum deductible, with lower premium). The choice of the franchise is annual and allows you to modulate the cost of coverage according to your personal needs. Those with reduced medical expenses can choose a high deductible and contain the monthly premium; those with chronic diseases or who often access benefits opt for a low deductible. The participation in expenses (copayment) is fixed at 10% after reaching the deductible (up to an annual ceiling of CHF 700 for outpatient medical costs only). The Italian CMI, an alternative for those who remain in the Italian system, is managed by INPS and covers the essential services of medicine - Net estimate: Use the [calcolatore di stipendio](nav:calculator) to enter the Swiss gross and see the approximate net (consider AVS 5.3%, ADD 1.1%, LPP 7–18%, source tax 6–13%, Italian deductible €10,000). - Cost of living: Compare rent, groceries and utilities in Mornago with your estimated net. A rule of thumb: Rent should not exceed 30% of your monthly net. - Health insurance: Request quotes from 2–3 LAMal insurers to compare premiums (CHF 300 vs CHF 2,500 franchise) and covered benefits. - Identity documents: Make sure your passport or ID card is valid for at least 6 months. The SEM may require criminal records or residency certificates. - Second language: If your Italian is not a native speaker, or if the canton of Ticino requires a language interview, prepare a certificate of linguistic competence (DALF, DELE, Goethe-Institut test, or notarial self-declaration). Next steps: Log in to [calcolatore di stipendio](nav:calculator) and enter your proposed gross. Compare the net with the monthly costs of accommodation, transport and food in Mornago. If the margin is comfortable, proceed with signing the contract and requesting the G Permit. Once you receive your AVS number, you can sign up for LAMal insurance and start working in Ticino with full social coverage.

item.title: Switzerland is losing its attractiveness for companies
item.description: Seven out of ten CEOs see a decline in Swiss attractiveness compared to international competition.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 70% of CEOs see a decline in Switzerland's attractiveness - Criticisms: regulation, taxation, infrastructure - Multinationals: 6% of businesses, 42% of GDP
## Key facts - **What**: Decline in Switzerland's economic attractiveness - When: Study published today - Where: Zurich - Who: McKinsey and Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce - Amount: 70% of CEOs, 42% of GDP
Switzerland is losing its appeal to companies. Seven out of ten CEOs see a deterioration compared to international competition. Regulation, taxation, and infrastructure are weighing heavily.
ZURICH - Seven out of ten business leaders believe that the Swiss economic hub is losing its advantages compared to international competition. This is according to a study published today by the consulting firm McKinsey and the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce. According to the report, the Confederation remains the leading European hub for research and development, but compared to the past, it attracts fewer global company headquarters and fewer international executives. 70% of the CEOs surveyed consider Switzerland's international attractiveness to be declining.
### Reported Criticisms Among the reported criticisms are the lengthening of approval procedures for investments in projects and work permits for foreign talent, cited by 70% of respondents, the introduction of the OECD minimum tax (65%), and infrastructure bottlenecks (60%). Managers also mention geopolitical tensions, new trade barriers, uncertainty in relations with the European Union, and the strength of the franc.
The study identifies five priority areas to preserve Switzerland's attractiveness in the long term: access to international talent, regulatory procedures, tax predictability, infrastructure, and strategic positioning vis-à-vis the EU, the United States, and Asia. According to the authors, a strong economic hub requires "efficient, proportionate, and predictable framework conditions that enable innovation, investment, and growth."
The report also highlights the weight of multinationals: although they represent only 6% of businesses in Switzerland, they generate 42% of Swiss GDP and are responsible for three-quarters of nominal economic growth since 2014. ## Implications for Frontiersmen The lengthening of investment approval procedures and work permits for foreign talent could affect companies' ability to attract and retain qualified personnel, including border workers. This could lead to more competition for jobs and a possible increase in bureaucracy for cross-border workers.
### Approval Procedures 70% of respondents reported a lengthening of investment approval procedures and work permits for foreign talent. This could mean longer times for obtaining work permits, affecting the mobility of cross-border workers.
### OECD Minimum Tax The introduction of the OECD minimum tax, reported by 65% of respondents, could have tax implications for companies and workers. This could affect Switzerland's tax competitiveness compared to other countries.
### Infrastructure Infrastructure bottlenecks, reported by 60% of respondents, could affect worker mobility and company logistics. This could lead to delays and additional costs for companies operating in Switzerland.

Here are some actions that can be taken:

### Planning Taxation Border workers should plan their taxation so that they are prepared for any tax changes, such as the introduction of the OECD minimum tax. This could include consulting tax advisors.

These tools can help border workers better understand the financial and tax implications of working in Switzerland.

item.title: Living in Gerenzano and working in Ticino: a guide for border workers
item.description: Distance, crossings, G permit, taxes, AVS and LAMal: everything you need to know before moving to Gerenzano from Ticino or other border areas.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Gerenzano is just a few km from the Ticino border, ideal for commuters to Lugano and Valle di Blenio - Permit G (cross-border worker) requires stable employment in Ticino and continuous residence in Italy - Withholding tax deducted in Switzerland; possible refunds through Italian declaration (quadro CE of the 730) - New cross-border agreement: effective from January 1, 2024, with a €10,000 allowance for new cross-border workers
## Key facts - **What**: Cross-border life between Gerenzano (Italy, province of Varese) and Ticino (Switzerland) - When: The new cross-border agreement is effective from January 1, 2024 - Where: Brogeda, Gaggiolo, Chiasso crossings for the Gerenzano–Ticino connection - Who: Permit G reserved for Italian residents who work stably in Switzerland - Amount: Annual €10,000 allowance for new cross-border workers (partial tax exemption)
Gerenzano, a municipality in the province of Varese less than 50 km from the Ticino border, is an increasingly popular choice for those who decide to work in Switzerland while remaining domiciled in Italy. The proximity to major cross-border crossings and the lower cost of living compared to the Swiss territory make this area attractive for cross-border workers seeking a balance between Swiss salary and Italian quality of life.
Anyone who decides to live in Gerenzano and work in Ticino must first understand the regime of Permit G (cross-border worker). This document, issued by the Swiss authorities, is exclusively reserved for Italian citizens who reside permanently in Italy and carry out dependent or independent work in Switzerland. Permit G is not automatic: it requires a work contract signed with a Ticino employer, verifiable work stability, and a fixed residence in the Italian municipality of residence.
### Taxation and taxation for the cross-border worker
One of the critical aspects for those living in Gerenzano and working in Ticino concerns the taxation of labor income. The fundamental rule is that the withholding tax is deducted exclusively in Switzerland, by the Ticino employer. Italy does not apply double taxation thanks to the tax credit system: the cross-border worker declares the Swiss income in the annual Italian declaration (Model 730), in quadro CE, and can recover part of the taxes paid in Switzerland.
From January 1, 2024, the new cross-border agreement signed on December 23, 2020, between Italy and Switzerland has introduced relevant novelties. New cross-border workers (those who started the activity after July 17, 2023) benefit from an annual allowance of €10,000 on the taxable Italian income. This allowance represents a partial exemption from regional and municipal taxes but does not eliminate the national tax on the first part of the income. The monthly payslip prepared in Switzerland will incur a withholding for Swiss federal tax, in addition to AVS/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% for the employee) and unemployment and accident insurance premiums. ### The Swiss contribution system and social security
For those working in Ticino, even if they live in Gerenzano, the payment of social security contributions follows Swiss rules. The AVS (Old Age and Survivors' Insurance) is mandatory from the first day of work: the contribution for the employee is 5.3% of the gross salary. In addition to the AVS, it is mandatory to join the disability insurance (AI) and unemployment insurance (IPG), both included in the same rate of 5.3%. Furthermore, for accident insurance (LAINF), the contribution varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the professional risk.
Many cross-border commuters are not aware that the second pillar (LPP, i.e., the Swiss supplementary pension scheme) is also mandatory for them. From the age of 25, the Swiss employer is required to contribute to the pension fund. This contribution, which varies between 7% and 18% of the salary depending on the age group and the company pension plan, represents a significant added value: at the time of retirement or transfer, the cross-border commuter will have access to a pension or accumulated capital that they would not have received in Italy.
### Health insurance and cross-border commuter rights
An often underestimated aspect concerns health insurance (LAMal). The cross-border commuter with a G permit has the **right of choice**: they can join the Ticino health system or remain insured with an Italian health insurance fund (CMI). The choice must be made consciously. If they choose to stay in Italy, they pay Italian insurance premiums and have coverage through the National Health Service for basic services, but they may be exposed in case of complex specialist care or planned interventions in Switzerland. If they choose the Ticino LAMal, they pay Swiss premiums (adults' deductible between CHF 300 and CHF 2500 annually depending on the chosen deductible), but they have access to excellent Swiss hospital facilities and broader coverage.
The Double Taxation Convention between Italy and Switzerland (signed on December 9, 1976) does not address the health matter; it mainly regulates double taxation on income. For this reason, the choice between LAMal and CMI remains a personal and legal decision based on awareness of the two options. Many cross-border commuters in their first year of activity do not have a clear picture of how these systems interact: communication between the Swiss employer, pension fund, and insurance can generate confusion.
### Renewal procedure and contractual changes
A crucial element that changes the perception of stability is the annual renewal of registration with the migration office (SEM). Although the G permit is defined as 'cross-border,' it is not unlimited: it requires an annual verification of the continuity of employment in Ticino. A change of job, prolonged unemployment, or a move to an Italian municipality further from the border can complicate the renewal. Consequently, those living in Gerenzano must maintain a stable relationship with the Ticino employer and ensure that the distance from the workplace remains compatible with the definition of 'cross-border.'
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Pre-move checklist
Before deciding to move to Gerenzano to work in Ticino, it is advisable to verify some concrete elements. First, consult the Ticino employer about the availability of administrative support: many large Ticino companies have established procedures for hiring cross-border workers and can facilitate the G permit application with the SEM.
Second, acquire the exact banking and tax coordinates. The cross-border worker must open a bank account that can receive salaries paid in CHF, but many Ticino accounts have minimum balance requirements or fees. In parallel, it is useful to verify in advance how to manage the Italian tax return: consult a chartered accountant or a tax consultant specialized in cross-border workers to understand the CE framework of the 730 and the tax return payment deadlines.
Third: choose the health insurance category. If you choose LAMal, contact a Ticino health insurance company directly (e.g., contact the canton or specialized intermediaries) to receive a personalized offer. If you remain in the Italian CMI, notify the insurer of any changes of residence and verify integrated cover between Italy and Switzerland.
### Border crossings and commuting times
The geographical position of Gerenzano allows access to three main border crossings: Brogeda (towards Mendrisio), Gaggiolo (towards Valle di Blenio), and Chiasso (towards Lugano). Travel times depend on the work destination in Ticino and traffic conditions. Under normal conditions, Gerenzano is approximately 45–80 minutes by car from the main Ticino cities (Lugano, Mendrisio, Bellinzona), depending on the road situation and the chosen border crossing. It is important to verify in advance the typical queues at the border crossings during peak hours (7–9 am and 5–7 pm) and consider, if possible, flexible working hours or telecommuting for some days of the week.
### Advantages and disadvantages of the Gerenzano–Ticino choice
**Main advantages**: gross salary typically 30–50% higher than in Italy, mandatory pension contributions (LPP) that guarantee a supplementary pension, access to excellent healthcare facilities, and lower cost of living in Italy (rent, food, services) compared to Ticino. The tax regime with a franchise for new cross-border workers reduces the tax burden compared to a pure Italian employee.
Disadvantages and risks: the G permit requires verifiable work continuity; dismissal or prolonged unemployment could jeopardize permit renewal. Daily commuting consumes time and fuel (annual Swiss vignette mandatory, approx. CHF 40). Administrative management is more complex: double tax returns, coordination between Swiss and Italian authorities, potential disputes over cross-border healthcare services. Finally, the volatility of the CHF/EUR exchange rate can impact real purchasing power when receiving in francs and spending in euros.
### Practical tools and resources
Before formalizing the move, use our tools to simulate the tax and pension impact. The [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to enter the Swiss gross salary and immediately see the AVS/AI/IPG deductions, federal taxes, and the monthly net amount. Alongside this, the [cost of living comparator](nav:cost-of-living) shows the real comparison between Gerenzano (Italian prices) and the main Ticino cities, helping you plan your family budget. Finally, consult the [refund guide](nav:ristorni) to discover how to maximize tax recovery through the annual Italian return.

## In brief - Permesso G allows daily commuting between Crosio della Valle and Ticino without Swiss residence - Withholding tax only in Switzerland from January 1, 2024 - Open borders: Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa towards Ticino - Lower cost of living in Italy, Swiss salary in CHF is advantageous
## Key facts - **What**: Permesso G for cross-border workers living in Italy and working in Switzerland - When: New Cross-Border Agreement in effect from January 1, 2024 - Where: Crosio della Valle (Italy) – Canton Ticino (Switzerland) - Who: Cross-border workers, Swiss and Italian administrations, employers - Tax: Withheld exclusively in Switzerland (tax credit in Italy) - Borders: Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa
Living in Crosio della Valle and working in Ticino is a strategic choice for thousands of cross-border workers. The Permesso G allows daily commuting without the need for permanent residence in Switzerland, while the cross-border tax regime (regulated by the New Cross-Border Agreement effective from January 1, 2024) offers concrete advantages on withholding tax: it is collected exclusively by Switzerland, and Italy avoids double taxation by automatically recognizing the tax credit in the CE section of the 730 declaration.
### Permesso G and daily commuting
The Permesso G allows an Italian citizen to work in Ticino without permanently residing in Switzerland. This means you can live in Crosio della Valle and cross the Ticino borders daily (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo or Ponte Tresa) to reach your workplace. You are not required to move your residence to Switzerland; you remain a resident in Italy, pay Italian municipal taxes in Crosio della Valle, and benefit from the Swiss cross-border tax structure.
This model is particularly convenient for those working in central or southern Ticino (Lugano, Mendrisio, Bellinzona). Travel times from the borders to the main industrial and tertiary areas of the canton Ticino vary depending on the destination and time of transit: traffic jams at the borders can significantly affect the total commuting time, especially during peak morning (7:00–9:00) and evening (17:00–19:00) hours.
### Taxation and withholding tax
From January 1, 2024, the New Cross-Border Agreement has simplified the mechanism for withholding tax on the employment income of Italian cross-border workers in Ticino. The withholding is made exclusively by Switzerland (by the employer or the Swiss administration), while Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit recognized in the CE section of the income tax return (model 730).
This means that on your Swiss pay slip, you will see the Swiss withholding tax deducted, but you will not see any further Italian withholdings. The added value is significant: you do not have to wait for a refund from the Revenue Agency to recover double-paid taxes. The Italian income tax return will automatically recognize the Swiss tax credit already paid, greatly simplifying cross-border tax management. ### Advantages and disadvantages of border choice
Choosing to live in Crosio della Valle and work in Ticino presents concrete pros and cons.
Advantages: The cost of living in Italy (rent, food, services) is typically lower than in Ticino. A Swiss salary in CHF maintains much higher purchasing power than an Italian salary in EUR, allowing you to save significantly. The Swiss social contribution (AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% paid by the employee, in addition to AD/AC 1.1% and LAINF 0.7-1.5% for the employer) translates into a more robust social security: access the AVS system (first Swiss pillar) and you can join the LPP (second pillar, professional insurance) with rates ranging from 7% to 18% depending on the age group (from 25 years). In addition, you retain the rights of residence and Italian communities: family, social network, local schools remain in Italy.
Disadvantages: Daily commuting involves vehicle wear, fuel costs, and above all loss of time and psychophysical fatigue. Queues at the passes (Brogeda, Chiasso, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa) can lengthen the journey by 30–60 minutes on busy days. Remain exposed to Italian legislation regarding municipal taxes, property taxes, and local services. Finally, if you change employer or your contract changes mode, you may lose the right to the G permit.

To live in Crosio della Valle and work in Ticino, follow these concrete steps:
1. Make sure you have a job contract in Ticino. The G permit is tied to employment: you need a job offer or a contract with a Swiss employer in the canton of Ticino. Without this documentation, your application will be rejected.
**2. Gather the required documents.** Identity documents (passport or Italian ID card), original employment contract, residence certificates, criminal records and pending charges certificates issued by the competent Italian authorities. Request these from the Municipality of Crosio della Valle and the relevant Police Headquarters. The Swiss employer will be part of the procedure: the communication to the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) of the Swiss Confederation must come from the Swiss authorities.
3. Submit the application through your employer. The Swiss employer will submit the G permit application to the competent Ticino cantonal authority (Division of Economy, Migration Section). You cannot submit the application personally from Italy; it is the employer who manages the Swiss administrative procedure.
4. Wait for approval. Approval times vary from 2 to 6 weeks. Once approved, you will receive the G permit (paper or digital document). The permit is personal and tied to the employer: if you change employers, you will need to apply for a new permit.
5. Registration with the Municipality of Crosio della Valle. Ensure that your residence in Italy is official with the Municipality of Crosio della Valle. The Municipality will have information on your cross-border employment and the importance of correct declaration for tax purposes.
### Tax deadlines to remember
Advance to April 30 for the Italian income tax declaration (730 or Unico, depending on the situation). Fill out the CE section accurately to declare Swiss income and the tax credit already paid in Switzerland. The Italian Revenue Agency and the cantonal authorities automatically exchange information on cross-border workers, so errors or omissions are easily identified. item.title: Riverlhab: the project that regenerates the Lura stream
item.description: Interreg Italy-Switzerland to renaturalize the Lura stream between Ticino and Varese. Cultural festival in Saronno 4-6 September and travelling exhibition in schools
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Riverlhab: Interreg project for the renaturalization of the Lura stream - Budget 1,5 million euros + 101.200 CHF; festival and itinerant exhibition - Canton Ticino and SUPSI partners; 162 people involved - Ri.Ver Festival in Saronno 4-6 September; exhibition curated by SUPSI
## Key facts - **What**: Interreg project for the renaturalization of the Lura stream and shared ecosystem management - When: Ongoing; Ri.Ver Festival 4-6 September in Saronno - Where: Lura stream between Canton Ticino and the province of Varese - Who: Consorzio Parco Lura (lead Como), ERSAF, Department of Territory Canton Ticino, SUPSI - Budget: EUR 1.476.620,34 + CHF 101.200 - Participants: 162 stakeholders and students involved - Intervention areas: 6 renaturalization zones along the stream
It is called Riverlhab and is the Interreg project that brings together Italy and Switzerland to address the renaturalization of the Lura stream, with the aim of tackling the impacts of climate change on river habitats in the border territory between the two countries. The lead is the Consorzio Parco del Lura, based in Como, while the partners include ERSAF, the Department of Territory of the Canton Ticino, and the Scuola Universitaria Professionale della Svizzera Italiana (SUPSI).
The total budget is 1.476.620,34 euros, to which a Swiss contribution of 101.200 francs is added. The heart of the project is the definition of common methodologies between Italy and Switzerland to intervene in the river basin sections where the relationship between the natural hydrographic network and the human-built environment becomes more complex. The idea is to build a shared and replicable ecosystem management model, actively involving both citizens and local public administrations, to improve the hydromorphological quality and ecosystem functionality of some sections of the Lura stream.
### Citizens as protagonists: exhibition, festival, and participatory monitoring
An important part of the project concerns the direct involvement of citizens. Activities of citizen science for the participatory monitoring of watercourses and wetlands are planned, both in the territory of the Parco del Lura and in the Canton Ticino, together with the involvement of associations, schools, and local administrators. The realization of an interactive and multimedia exhibition, curated by the Institute of Design of SUPSI, is designed to deepen the themes of territorial instability and the dynamics of rivers. The exhibition will be itinerant and easily transportable, so that it can be hosted in schools, civic centers, and libraries of both territories.
This is accompanied by the transnational cultural festival – the Ri.Ver Festival – whose first edition will take place in Saronno from 4 to 6 September. The realization of a 'narrative game' is also planned to bring citizens closer to the knowledge of their territory and the good practices of river management, as well as days of cleaning and other activities of citizen activation. [Search for participation opportunities in SUPSI projects](nav:jobs) ### Comparison tables and sharing of best practices
The project involves the organization of comparison tables between the different stakeholders involved: Municipalities, provinces, Lombardy Region, ERSAF, local Civil Protection groups, water service managers, as well as the Canton of Ticino with the Office of Watercourses and the Environment Division. The objective is to study and share best practices in the management of river areas already experienced in both territories. This cross-border approach allows for a direct comparison between Italian and Swiss experiences, with the possibility of adopting innovative strategies tested in similar contexts.
For local technicians and administrators, the project offers a specific training path focused on integrated design through Nature Based Solutions and adaptation strategies to climate change. The training will include introductory meetings, technical-scientific and managerial modules, in-person and remote workshops, site visits, and the creation of an educational manual. Four public meetings on climate change and active citizenship are also planned. This training approach involves both professionals in the hydraulic and environmental sectors and local administrations in Ticino and Lombardy.
### Territorial experimentation and the role of SUPSI
The most concrete part of Riverlhab concerns the experimentation of specific interventions for the renaturalization of riverbanks. Six project areas have been identified along the course of the Lura stream, where widespread territorial interventions will be carried out. Each will have specific local objectives but with significant impacts on the entire river valley.
In this phase, students from the SUPSI Institute of Design will also be involved, tasked with designing viewing points and overlooks on the river as part of their educational path. This aspect transforms the project into a training opportunity also for the Ticino university system, with future designers who can contribute concretely to the regeneration of the territory and develop practical skills in the field of environmental design.
Overall, the project aims to involve and train 162 people, including local stakeholders and students, by its conclusion. The activities carried out will lead to two main results at the cross-border level: a common strategy for the involvement of citizens in the care and protection of their territory, and a shared methodology for the requalification and renaturalization of the stretches of the Lura stream. The ultimate goal is to mitigate the impacts of climate change on river habitats even beyond the conclusion of the project. [Discover the training opportunities for administrators and technicians](nav:jobs)

The Ri.Ver Festival, the first edition of the cross-border cultural festival, will take place in Saronno from September 4 to 6. This event represents the ideal opportunity for citizens, administrators, and environmental sector operators to delve into the project's themes and discover the cross-border territory from a new perspective. The festival will connect the two territories and bring to the attention of the communities the themes of river regeneration and shared environmental management.
For those who cannot reach Saronno, the itinerant exhibition represents an alternative to discover the project. Curated by the SUPSI Institute of Design, the interactive and multimedia exhibition will be hosted in schools, civic centers, and libraries of both territories. This itinerant format allows reaching a wider audience, from schools to local communities, to raise awareness on the themes of territorial decay and river dynamics. The portability of the exhibition ensures that even the smallest centers of the cross-border territory can benefit from this educational resource.
Active participation and training opportunities
In addition to the exhibition, days of cleaning the stream and other activities to activate citizenship are planned, as well as a 'narrative game' to bring citizens closer to the knowledge of their territory and good practices of river management. These initiatives also allow non-specialists to contribute concretely to environmental care and feel protagonists of the regeneration of their territory.
For interested local administrators and technicians, the project offers introductory meetings, technical-scientific modules, in-person and remote workshops, site visits, and the creation of an educational manual. SUPSI students also have the opportunity to participate in a summer school and contribute directly to the design of the river viewpoints. To stay informed about the dates and participation methods for the Ri.Ver Festival events, citizen science activities, and training courses, consult the project's official channels or contact the Consorzio Parco del Lura. Do not miss the opportunity to discover how your cross-border territory is regenerating and how to actively contribute to this transformation. item.title: San Siro and Ticino: A Guide for Commuters
item.description: G Permit, Withholding Tax, Tax Rebates, and the New 2024 Agreement. Everything you need to know to work in Ticino from San Siro.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - **G Permit** required for cross-border workers employed in Ticino - Withholding tax deducted only in Switzerland; no double taxation - New agreement effective January 1, 2024: tax refunds ranging from CHF 7,500 (under the old system) to CHF 10,000 (under the new system) - AVS/LPP/LAMal: Swiss contributions and entitlements for Italian residents
## Key Facts - What: Tax and social security regime for cross-border workers in the Canton of Ticino - When: New Cross-Border Workers Agreement effective January 1, 2024 (ratified in Italy: Law 83/2023) - Where: Ticino, Switzerland — residence in Italy (e.g., San Siro, Lombardy) - Who: Italian employees with a G permit - Amount: Minimum refund of CHF 7,500 (existing cross-border workers), CHF 10,000 (new cross-border workers) - Legal Basis: Italian-Swiss Agreement of December 9, 1976; New Agreement signed December 23, 2020
A cross-border worker who resides in San Siro or any municipality in Lombardy and works as an employee in Ticino must hold a G permit, the document that authorizes foreign nationals to work as employees in Switzerland. The permit is valid for one year and must be renewed before it expires.
On January 1, 2024, the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and ratified by Italy through Law No. 83 of June 13, 2023, entered into force. This agreement has modified the tax regime and tax refunds for those who cross the Ticino border daily.
### The Key Principle: Withholding Tax Only in Switzerland
A crucial aspect that protects cross-border workers: withholding tax is deducted ONLY by the Ticino employer from the gross salary. Italy does not impose a second tax on foreign income thanks to the tax credit provided for in Section CE of Form 730. The Italian-Swiss Convention of December 9, 1976, guarantees this mechanism: the Italian Revenue Agency recognizes taxes paid in Switzerland and applies a tax credit to avoid double taxation.
Long-term cross-border workers (those who were already working as such before July 17, 2023) are eligible for an annual exemption of CHF 7,500 on a transitional basis until 2033. New cross-border workers have an annual tax-free allowance of CHF 10,000. This tax protection is the main reason why the cross-border worker regime remains advantageous compared to other employment options.
[Leggi la guida sui permessi frontalieri per sapere come richiederlo](nav:permits) ### Mandatory Swiss Social Security Contributions: AVS, LPP, and Other Insurance Programs
Cross-border employees working in Ticino do not only pay withholding tax; they are also required to contribute to the Swiss social security systems according to federal rates. These amounts are withheld from their paycheck by the employer.
- AVS (Old Age and Survivors’ Insurance): 5.3% of gross wages (employee’s share) - AI (Disability Insurance): included in the AVS percentage - IPG (Public Holiday Allowance): 5.3% - Unemployment (AD) and Disaster Relief (AC): 1.1% (with an annual cap of CHF 148,200) - LAINF (Accident Insurance): 0.7–1.5% depending on the industry - LPP (Occupational Pension Plan): 7–18% depending on age (from age 25 onward)
The total amount of these contributions (approximately 15–25% of gross pay) is less than what a cross-border worker would pay if they were a resident of Switzerland and an ordinary taxpayer. However, they acquire full Swiss social security and insurance rights: old-age and disability pensions, as well as health and accident benefits recognized by the FSO (Federal Statistical Office) and administered by SUVA and recognized LPP funds.
### The Italian Income Tax Return: Form CE and Tax Credit
Every cross-border worker must report income earned in Switzerland to the Italian Revenue Agency. Employees file Form 730, while self-employed professionals file Form Unico. The key section is the CE section (Credits for Taxes Paid Abroad).
How the credit works: The Italian Revenue Agency compares the withholding tax paid in Switzerland with the Italian IRPEF tax rate that would apply to the same income. The Italian tax rates are: - 23% up to EUR 28,000 - 35% from EUR 28,001 to EUR 50,000 - 43% above EUR 50,000
If the Swiss tax is lower, the cross-border worker receives a tax credit (a reduction in the Italian tax). If it is higher, they do not pay any additional tax in Italy. In both cases, the tax credit mechanism prevents double taxation.
[Calcola il tuo netto svizzero con il simulatore di busta paga](nav:payslip)
### LAMal: Choosing Between Italian and Swiss Health Insurance
Cross-border workers in Category G have the right to choose between Italian health insurance (administered by INPS and the Lombardy region) and Swiss health insurance (LAMal). This choice is binding for the calendar year and must be made with full knowledge of the facts: Swiss LAMal involves adult deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 depending on the coverage selected, while Italian health insurance has different deductibles and mechanisms.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Step-by-Step Guide: How to Start Working in Ticino
Step 1: Apply for a G permit Contact the Migration Office (SEM) of the canton where you will be working in Ticino (e.g., SEM Ticino for the south, SEM Graubünden/Valais if elsewhere). The permit must be renewed annually. Required documents: - Valid identification document (passport or ID card) - Employment contract signed by your Ticino employer - Proof of residence in Italy (San Siro or another municipality) - If necessary, a certificate of no criminal record (depending on the canton)
Step 2: Register with the INPS as a cross-border worker The Italian INPS must be aware of your cross-border worker status in order to recognize the contributions you’ve made in Switzerland as part of your insurance history. Apply for a specific registration; this facilitates the recognition of AVS/AI contributions toward your future Italian pension and the exchange of information with Swiss authorities.
Step 3: Complete the annual tax return By May 31 (according to the Italian Revenue Agency’s calendar), file Form 730 or Unico with the CE section completed. Attach: - Certificate from the Swiss source (receipt of withholdings made by the employer) - Pay stubs proving AVS/AI/LPP contributions - Declaration of non-residency in Switzerland (if you opted for the Italian LAMal)
Step 4: Tax Refund and Tax Credit Starting in 2024, if you are a cross-border worker, the tax refund will follow the new agreement. Existing cross-border workers benefit from an annual exemption of CHF 7,500; new cross-border workers benefit from an annual exemption of CHF 10,000. The credit is processed through the Italian Revenue Agency or, in some cases, through the Lombardy Region. Check the Revenue Agency’s website or contact a CAF for exact timelines.
Before signing a contract with a Ticino-based employer, verify the following: - Is the employer properly registered with the Ticino cantonal authorities? - Which canton issues the G permit (this depends on the company’s headquarters)? - Are you able to cross the border daily (Gaggiolo, Brogeda, Chiasso)? - Do you prefer to keep your Italian health insurance or opt for Swiss LAMal? (Decide before signing) - Do you have valid and up-to-date identification documents?
[Scopri le tue opzioni di copertura sanitaria: LAMal vs Italia](nav:health)
The [calcolatore fiscale per frontalieri](nav:calculator) tool allows you to simulate your Ticino pay stub, taking into account AVS, withholding tax, social security contributions, and tax rebates, so you can determine in advance your net pay and assess the financial benefits of your choice.
