item.title: Living in Inverigo, working in Ticino: border guide
item.description: Distance, taxation, G permit, LAMal and costs: everything you need before moving to Inverigo working in Ticino as a border worker.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Inverigo (Como) a few km from the Ticino border: direct connection to the crossings - Tax at source withheld only in Switzerland; refunds by Italian declaration 730 - G Permit, LAMal with option right, Swiss AVS/LPP with INPS integration
## Key facts - **What**: Living in Inverigo (Lombardy) and working in Ticino with G border permit - Where: Inverigo, province of Como — Canton of Ticino, Switzerland - Tax Agreement: New Frontier Agreement, in force from 1 January 2024 (signed 23 December 2020) - Tax at source: Withheld by the Swiss employer, tax credit in Italian declaration - Deductibles: Old frontier workers (pre 17/7/2023): exemption €7,500 transitional regime 2024–2033; new frontier workers: €10,000
Inverigo, a municipality in the province of Como in Lombardy, is strategically positioned for those who want to live in Italy while maintaining a stable job in Ticino. The proximity to the Swiss border — connected by the Brogeda, Chiasso and Gaggiolo crossings — makes this solution viable for professionals and frontier workers looking for a balance between housing costs and work opportunities across borders.
Border taxation follows a well-established principle: income tax at source is exclusively withheld in Switzerland by the employer. Italy recognises this payment through the tax credit, regulated in an annual declaration (form 730, EC framework). Balanced taxation: how the Italian-Swiss system works
The frontier taxation for those living in Inverigo and working in Ticino is structured on two levels. The gross income received in Switzerland is subject to a withholding tax calculated according to the Swiss federal rates, plus contributions for AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% total for the employee), AD/AC (1.1% up to the cap of CHF 148'200), and LAINF (0.7–1.5% depending on the sector). These payments are mandatory and are managed by the employer.
In Italy, the frontier worker declares the gross Swiss income in the model 730 (quadro CE) and applies the ordinary IRPEF rates (23% up to €28'000, 35% for the second bracket €28'001–50'000, 43% for incomes over €50'000). However, the Italian Revenue Agency applies a tax credit for the Swiss withholdings already paid, balancing the overall taxation and avoiding full double taxation. The result is an effective rate that reflects the weighted average between the Swiss and Italian systems.
For old frontier workers (those who had the status before July 17, 2023), the €7'500 exemption in the transitional regime until 2033 mitigates the transition to the new system. New frontier workers benefit from a €10'000 allowance. These exemption margins further reduce the Italian taxable base.
Cost of living: Inverigo vs. Ticino
Lombardy, and in particular the province of Como, offers a significantly lower cost of living compared to Ticino. Rents, food, services, and utilities are on average 20–30% cheaper in Inverigo compared to urban centers in Ticino such as Lugano, Bellinzona, or Locarno. For a family or a single person looking to optimize their monthly budget, this difference is substantial: a rent of CHF 1'200–1'500 in Ticino corresponds to about €800–1'000 in Inverigo.
However, the frontier worker should not forget the commuting costs: Swiss vignette (annual, mandatory to circulate on Swiss roads), fuel for daily trips to the border and to the workplace, and possibly tolls if using the A9 Como-Chiasso and the A2 to reach destinations further north. Check the [waiting times at the Brogeda, Chiasso, and Gaggiolo border crossings](nav:border) during peak hours (7–9 am, 5–7 pm), as queues directly impact fuel consumption and quality of life.
Pension contributions and benefits
Swiss payments for AVS (5.3%), AI/IPG (5.3%), AD/AC (1.1%), LAINF (0.7–1.5%), and LPP (Professional Pension, 7–18% depending on age) accredit the frontier worker with rights to Swiss benefits: old-age/invalidity pension according to federal regulations, unemployment benefits (Unemployment Insurance). Italian-Swiss legislation provides for the accreditation of contribution periods in one of the two countries towards the calculation of the overall pension. Your INPS statement automatically integrates the Swiss periods. [Check how to integrate contribution periods in both countries for pension calculation](nav:pension) through the INPS online services or a consultant.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Practical checklist: how to get started
Before moving to Inverigo and starting to work in Ticino as a cross-border commuter, some specific steps are required. Here is the step-by-step procedure.
Step 1: Request for Permit G The residence permit for cross-border commuters (Permit G) is requested to the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) through the Swiss employer or a specialized agency. The SEM processes the application in coordination with the cantonal authorities (Population Office of the Canton Ticino). The permit is linked to the job and has a multi-year validity. Processing times vary, but they usually take 4–8 weeks. Required documents: identification, employment contract, certificate of no criminal record.
Step 2: Registration with AVS and insurance Once employed, the employer automatically registers the cross-border commuter with the competent cantonal AVS office. The cross-border commuter receives an AVS number (13 digits) used throughout their working career in Switzerland. The employer applies family allowances (if applicable according to the Canton), pays contributions for AVS/AI/IPG/AD/AC/LAINF and LPP according to the current rates, and provides the employee with a monthly payslip indicating all deductions.
Step 3: Choosing LAMal coverage Within 3 months of starting employment, the cross-border commuter chooses whether to enroll with a Swiss LAMal insurer (with a deductible from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 for adults) or to maintain Italian coverage with INPS with Swiss integration. The choice affects the cost of the premium, deductibles, and the network of healthcare facilities that can be used. [Use the LAMal comparison tools](nav:health) to evaluate the options available in your Canton of work.
Step 4: Italian tax declaration and refunds Each year, the cross-border commuter completes the 730 form with the Revenue Agency, a CAF (Tax Assistance Center), or online through the Revenue Agency's Entratel portal. In the CE section (foreign income section), they report: gross income received in Switzerland, withholding tax deductions, amounts paid for AVS and other contributions. INPS verifies the pension integration; the declaration generates refunds (amounts in favor of the cross-border commuter) or payments to settle the overall taxation. Deadline: usually by April 30 of the following year.
Step 5: Financial planning and using the calculator Before moving, calculate the net monthly income in CHF after all Swiss deductions, compare it with the monthly costs in Inverigo (rent, utilities, groceries, transportation), and assess whether the margin is sustainable. [Use the cross-border salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the net monthly income based on your proposed gross salary. Include in the budget: annual Swiss vignette (about CHF 40), estimated fuel for commuting, car insurance, LAMal or INPS (monthly premiums), and a reserve for unexpected expenses.
### When the move is worth it: final evaluation Living in Inverigo and working in Ticino is worth it when: (a) the monthly cost of living in Inverigo, including commuting, is significantly lower than the net income received in CHF; (b) the job in Ticino offers competitive salaries and contractual stability; (c) you are willing to manage daily commuting times (30–60 minutes depending on the Ticino destination). The balanced taxation between the two countries, thanks to the tax credit system and cross-border exemptions, protects income from double taxation.
Final steps: Calculate your net monthly income and compare it with the living costs in Inverigo using the available tools. Verify travel times from the border crossings to your future workplace, consider the quality of life (schools, healthcare, local transportation), and consult a tax advisor to clarify your specific case of transition to the new cross-border regime 2024.

item.title: Living in Cambiasca, working in Ticino: frontier guide
item.description: Taxation, G permit, costs and concrete procedures for border workers living in Cambiasca and working in the Canton of Ticino. What you need to know.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- New Cross-Border Agreement effective from 1 January 2024: withholding tax deducted ONLY in Switzerland - Italian tax refunds through tax credit (section CE of the 730 form): no double taxation - Exemption €7,500 (old cross-border workers 2024–2033) or €10,000 (new); AVS/AI 5.3% for employees - Permit G required; LAMal optional with deductible CHF 300–2500 for adults
## Key facts
- **Who**: Cross-border workers residing in Italy, employed in the Canton of Ticino - Permit: Permit G according to the Convention of 9 December 1976 and the New Agreement of 23/12/2020 - Effective date: 1 January 2024 (Italian ratification: Law 83 of 13/6/2023) - Tax: Deducted in Switzerland; Italian tax credit in section CE - Exemption: €7,500 (cross-border workers since 17/7/2023) or €10,000 (new); transitional period 2024–2033 - Contributions: AVS/AI 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7–1.5%, LPP 7–18% - Insurance: LAMal optional; deductible for adults CHF 300–2500
### 2024 Agreement: What changes for cross-border workers
The New Cross-Border Agreement, signed on 23 December 2020 and effective from 1 January 2024, introduces verified rules on taxation. The Italian part (Law 83 of 13/6/2023) and the Swiss part have defined the methods of withholding tax collection. The Italian-Swiss Convention on double taxation (9 December 1976) remains the underlying legal framework. For those living in Cambiasca and working in Ticino, the change is concrete: the tax on the paycheck is withheld directly in Switzerland by the employer. Italy does not levy further taxes but recognizes a tax credit in section CE of the 730 declaration, thus avoiding double taxation.
The exemption depends on when one became a cross-border worker. Those who were cross-border workers before 17 July 2023 benefit from an annual exemption of €7,500 for the transitional period 2024–2033. Those who become cross-border workers after that date are entitled to an exemption of €10,000. This change in regime is one of the most significant points of the 2024 agreement. In 2033, the transitional regime ends and all cross-border workers move to the ordinary regime.
### Contributions and AVS: How the paycheck works
In Switzerland, from the gross paycheck, the AVS/AI/IPG contributions are deducted at 5.3% for the employee. Then there is unemployment insurance (AD/AC) at 1.1% on a maximum annual basis of CHF 148,200, and accident insurance (LAINF) between 0.7% and 1.5%. If the cross-border worker has professional pension insurance (LPP, second pillar), they contribute a percentage between 7% and 18% depending on age (from 25 years onwards). All these deductions are managed by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV) according to the federal and cantonal rates established by law. A cross-border worker living in Cambiasca and working in Ticino follows the same scheme: the AVS pension amount will be calculated on the contributions paid in Switzerland, not on the Italian ones.
[Net salary calculator](nav:calculator) ### Withholding tax: how NOT to end up in double taxation
A cross-border worker living in Cambiasca receives their pay slip from their Ticino-based employer. The Swiss withholding tax has already been applied to this pay slip according to cantonal and federal tables. This tax is not collected simultaneously in Italy. When the cross-border worker files their 730 tax return in Italy (by June of the following year), they report their foreign income in the CE section. The Italian Revenue Agency recognizes the tax credit (i.e., the fact that Switzerland has already deducted it), thus avoiding double taxation. If the Swiss tax is higher than the Italian tax, the cross-border worker receives a refund; if it is lower, they pay the difference.
Swiss tax rates vary at the federal and cantonal levels, but the cross-border worker does not choose the amount: it is applied by the Ticino-based employer according to the current AFC/ESTV tables. The result is that the net monthly income of a cross-border worker living in Cambiasca may be lower than that of a worker residing in Switzerland, with the same gross income, because the Ticino cantonal withholding is often higher than the national average.
### Old and new cross-border workers: different regimes until 2033
Were you a cross-border worker before July 17, 2023? You benefit from a transitional regime (2024–2033) with an exemption of €7,500 on your taxable income in Italy. Did you become a cross-border worker after that date? Your exemption is €10,000. The difference is measured, but significant:
- **Old cross-border worker**: With a gross Swiss income of €50,000, the €7,500 exemption reduces the Italian taxable base to €42,500. - New cross-border worker: Same situation, but with €10,000 exempt = Italian taxable base €40,000.
This protection is gradually phased out by 2033, when even old cross-border workers will switch to the ordinary regime without exemption. Until then, the transitional regime protects those who were already commuting at the time of the 2024 Agreement. It is a political choice not to penalize those who had already organized their lives around that tax system.
[Guide to tax refunds](nav:ristorni)
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### First step: request the Permesso G
To work in Ticino and live in Cambiasca, you need a valid Permesso G. The permit is issued by the cantonal migration office of Ticino (SEM - State Secretariat for Migration at the Swiss level; at the cantonal level, it is the Immigration Office of the Canton of Ticino). The request usually goes through the employer: they notify the Swiss authorities of the hiring, who then initiate the procedure. You, as an Italian employee residing in Italy, provide the required documents (identity, employment contract, certificate of no criminal record). The Permesso G is free and has limited validity (usually 1 year, renewable).
The Italian-Swiss Convention of December 9, 1976 recognizes the right of citizens to work across the border. Your right to work in Ticino is protected by this legal instrument. However, from January 1, 2024, the new regime of the Cross-Border Workers Agreement modifies the tax obligations (as described in the previous paragraphs), not the permit obligations. The Permesso G remains the main instrument for cross-border work.
### Pay slip, 730 declaration and tax credit
Each month you will receive the pay slip with the withholding tax deducted. Keep all original pay slips (paper or digital). During the fiscal year, Switzerland (through the employer or the AFC/ESTV) will communicate to your Revenue Agency the amount of gross income and withheld tax. By June of the following year, you submit the 730 model online (through the tax agency, accountant, or CAF). In the CE section of the 730, you report the foreign income and tax paid in Switzerland. The Agency recognizes the Swiss tax credit and calculates the Italian tax due. The refund or balance is managed as for any ordinary 730 declaration.
### Health insurance and LAMal choice
Living in Italy but working in Switzerland, you have the option to choose Swiss health insurance (LAMal, Health Insurance Law). You are not obliged: you can keep the Italian insurance (INPS). If you choose Swiss LAMal, you must subscribe to it with a Swiss health insurance fund. The deductibles for adults range from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 per year (the rest of the costs are covered by the fund until the deductible is reached, then the system covers 90% of the expenses). Choosing LAMal also means paying the premiums directly to the health insurance fund, not through the salary. According to the Health Insurance Law, those in category G (cross-border workers) can exercise this option.
[LAMal health insurance](nav:health)
### Online tools to calculate net income and refunds
Use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) of Frontaliere Ticino to estimate the monthly withholding tax and the annual net income. Enter the Swiss gross income, the canton of work (Ticino), your category (cross-border worker G), and the fiscal year. The tool applies the federal and cantonal rates according to the 2024 regime and your cross-border worker status. For a more accurate estimate of Italian tax refunds, consult the dedicated guide to refunds on this site: it explains how to read the 730 model and predict any tax refunds or balances due.

item.title: Living in Cocquio-Trevisago as a Ticino border worker: guide 2024
item.description: Moving from Cocquio-Trevisago to work in Ticino: the New Frontier Agreement 2024, tax at source, exemptions €7500–€10000 and step-by-step procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New Cross-Border Workers Agreement effective from January 1, 2024: changes to the tax regime - Withholding tax deducted ONLY in Switzerland, double taxation avoided - Old cross-border workers: exemption of €7500 annually (transitional 2024–2033) - New cross-border workers: allowance of €10000 annually
## Key facts - **What**: New tax regime for cross-border workers Italy-Switzerland with updated agreement - When: Effective from January 1, 2024 - Where: Canton Ticino and province of Varese (e.g., Cocquio-Trevisago) - Who: Cross-border workers with Permit G residing in Italy, working in Ticino - Exemption amount: €7500 annually (old cross-border workers 2024–2033) - Allowance amount: €10000 annually (new cross-border workers) - Tax treatment: Deducted ONLY in Switzerland; double taxation avoided through Italian tax credit in the CE section
Cocquio-Trevisago, a municipality in the province of Varese located a few kilometers from the Ticino border, is a recurring choice for cross-border workers who work in Canton Ticino. The geographical location offers access to major crossings and proximity to Ticino companies, but the decision to move requires a precise understanding of the current tax regime.
With the entry into force of the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement on January 1, 2024, the regulatory framework has undergone significant changes compared to the previous situation. The agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of June 13, 2023, redefines the taxation methods for workers residing in Italy and working in Switzerland.
A central element concerns the place of withholding tax: for cross-border workers, the withholding is made exclusively in Switzerland. Italy thus avoids double taxation through the mechanism of the tax credit in the CE section of the income tax return (model 730), provided for by the Italy-Switzerland Convention signed on December 9, 1976.
### The distinction between old and new cross-border workers
The regime provides a distinction depending on the date on which the status of cross-border worker was acquired. Those who were already working in Ticino before July 17, 2023 (old cross-border workers) benefit from an annual exemption up to €7500 within a transitional regime that lasts until 2033. New cross-border workers, i.e., those who started after that date, have a higher annual allowance: €10000. This distinction has direct implications on the paycheck: at equal gross income, the withholding varies based on the status acquired at the time of transfer. For those considering moving from Cocquio-Trevisago to Ticino, correctly identifying their category is the first operational step. ## Tax and social security implications for cross-border workers
Switching from an Italian to a Swiss salary involves changes in the structure of contributions and taxation. Unlike Italy, where the federal IRPEF is structured on progressive rates (23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000), Switzerland applies a withholding tax system managed at the federal and cantonal levels.
For the cross-border worker with Permit G, the Swiss contribution burden consists of: - **AVS/AI/IPG** (old-age, disability, and loss of earnings insurance): 5.3% of gross salary at the employee's expense - AD/AC (unemployment insurance and insolvency allowance): 1.1% with a maximum cap of CHF 148,200 of taxable income - LAINF (accident insurance): 0.7–1.5%, generally paid by the employer - LPP (mandatory second pillar pension): 7–18% depending on the age bracket from 25 years onwards
These contributions are deducted directly from the Swiss paycheck. A simulation with the [tax calculator](nav:calculator) shows that, at equal gross income, the Swiss net after deductions is often higher than the Italian net, also thanks to the double taxation credit system.
### Health insurance and social protection
An often underestimated aspect concerns health insurance (LAMal). Cross-border workers with Permit G have the right to choose: they can remain in the Italian system or opt for Swiss insurance. Adult deductibles in Switzerland range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually, depending on the chosen policy. Understanding the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) between Varese/Cocquio-Trevisago and Ticino is essential to evaluate the real economic advantage of the move: higher salaries in CHF must be weighed against housing, transportation, insurance, and food costs in the Canton of Ticino.
Regarding the [second and third pension pillars](nav:pension), those working in Switzerland are automatically enrolled in the LPP (mandatory) and have the option to subscribe to the third pillar (3a). These mechanisms build a pension capital significantly different from what is accumulated with INPS enrollment in Italy. The appreciation of the LPP fund during working life and the lifelong pension from Switzerland exceed the guarantees of the Italian pension system. Additionally, voluntary contributions to the third pillar offer immediate tax benefits in Switzerland not available in Italy. Those moving their residence must coordinate these positions with their [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to evaluate the net pension advantage.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## Pre-move procedure and checklist
Deciding to move from Cocquio-Trevisago to Ticino to work requires coordinated administrative planning. Here are the essential steps:
Step 1: Obtain the Permit G The Work Permit for cross-border commuters (Permit G) is the legal basis for working in Switzerland. It must be requested from the competent cantonal authorities of Ticino before starting work. The application generally includes the employment contract, identity documents, and proof of residence in Italy.
Step 2: Verify cross-border commuter status (old/new) Determining whether you fall into the category of "old cross-border commuters" (already in status before July 17, 2023) or "new cross-border commuters" is crucial. This distinction determines the annual exemption (€7500 vs. €10000) and directly affects the calculation of the Swiss payroll withholding.
Step 3: Notify the change of residence to the Tax Agency If you remain resident in Italy but work in Switzerland, you must notify the cross-border employment relationship to the Italian tax authorities. This allows the application of the tax credit in the CE section of the annual declaration (model 730 or Unico).
**Step 4: Choose health insurance** Exercise the LAMal option right: stay in the Italian system or switch to a Swiss policy with CHF 300–2500 deductibles. The decision depends on the individual health profile and the costs compared between the two systems.
### Tax timeline and deadlines
The move should be planned considering administrative times (obtaining Permit G: typically 2–4 weeks) and the first withholding calculation at the start of employment. The annual tax declaration in Italy (model 730 or Unico) includes the CE section for the tax credit on taxes paid in Switzerland. This declaration allows the cross-border commuter to recover, in the refund or compensation phase, the part of the Swiss tax not aligned with the Italian rates of their income bracket.
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) before moving to estimate the actual net monthly and annual income. Consult the [Permit G comparator](nav:permits) to verify the specific Ticino cantonal procedure. Accurate planning in the months preceding the move avoids tax surprises and ensures a smooth management of the dual administrative dimension (Italy-Switzerland) of cross-border life.

item.title: EoC hospitals in Ticino: ANQ research detects lights and shadows
item.description: The national ANQ survey rewards Ticino hospitals (75% satisfied patients), but indicates margins for improvement in communication during waits.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The ANQ 2025 survey involves 1,821 patients discharged from EOC hospitals - 75% report a positive experience, in line with the Swiss average - Critical issues: insufficient communication during admission wait times - Larger hospitals (Lugano, Bellinzona) report more problems
## Key facts - **What**: National survey on the quality of hospital stays (ANQ) - When: Patients discharged September-November 2025 - Where: Hospitals of the Ente ospedaliero cantonale (EOC), Ticino - Who: ANQ (national quality control body) + Adriana Degiorgi (head of EOC Quality Service) - Sample: 1,821 EOC patients out of 47,000 total in 186 Swiss facilities - Satisfaction: 75% positive experience - Main critical issue: Communication during admission wait times
The national ANQ research confirms an overall positive result for the Ticino Ente ospedaliero cantonale (EOC): three out of four patients report a positive experience of the stay, aligning with the Swiss average. But the study highlights a critical area for intervention: communication during wait times in the admission phase.
The survey involved 47,000 patients from 186 Swiss facilities, including 1,821 people discharged from EOC hospitals between September and November 2025. For the first time, the national questionnaire changed perspective, moving from measuring satisfaction to evaluating the patient's experience, "from admission to discharge," according to Adriana Degiorgi, head of the EOC Quality and Risk Service.
### Positive results The new questionnaire offers a much more granular view: about 40 questions compared to the 5 of the previous survey. Among the positive data, the research highlights how the EOC achieves results above the national average in explaining the use of new drugs. This aspect represents a strength: patients receive clear and timely information on prescribed treatments, reassured about the methods of administration and possible side effects.
### Emerging critical issues The critical node concerns communication during wait times in the hospital. Degiorgi observes: "The patient who expects to go to the ward within a certain time and cannot go, and no one says anything, is not good." The same dynamic repeats for those who need to undergo surgery: the patient arrives at the hospital in the morning, expects to enter the operating room within a set hour, but is postponed without receiving adequate updates. It is precisely here that the EOC recognizes a concrete margin for improvement. Those who live in Italy and work in Ticino [with Permit G](nav:permits), or who choose to access Ticino's healthcare services through their own [health insurance](nav:health), should consider these data when evaluating their expected hospital experience. The research highlights that, although the overall level is satisfactory, communication issues can negatively impact the perception of those already in a vulnerable situation during hospitalization or surgery. The hospital experience is not just a medical issue, but also an organizational and psychological one. When the patient does not receive communication about delays, anxiety increases and trust in the system erodes. For the cross-border worker who lives in Italy but works in Ticino, this communication issue becomes even more relevant: any postponements of interventions or prolonged waits require coordinating days off work, cross-border travel, and managing absence from the Italian territory. ### Larger Hospitals, Greater Challenges The results are not uniform across different EOC sites. The greatest challenges emerge in the larger hospitals: Bellinzona and Lugano, which manage a wider caseload and patients with more complex clinical situations. Degiorgi points out that this trend is not exclusive to Ticino: "We see it at the Swiss level across the entire survey: university hospitals or large hospitals often fare a bit worse compared to the Swiss benchmark." The organizational complexity of large hospitals—with more numerous departments, more patients hospitalized simultaneously, more surgical procedures—partly explains this discrepancy. But the risk is that the patient experience worsens precisely in hospitals where medical complexity is highest and where transparent communication would be most important. ### Data from Smaller Hospitals Aquarossa and Faido do not appear in the comparative analysis: overall, they have recorded fewer than 20 completed questionnaires, an insufficient number to derive statistically comparable results. However, the absence of evident issues in smaller hospitals suggests that more direct communication and less congested logistics could have positive effects on patient perception. The ANQ research thus provides a two-speed snapshot of the Canton of Ticino: the territory is in line with the national average, but the gap between large and small hospitals reflects a broader organizational challenge of the Swiss healthcare system.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How to intervene as a patient
If during a stay in an EOC hospital you encounter communication problems during waiting times – no updates on times, unexplained delays, uncertainty about procedures – you have the right to report it. The ANQ survey works precisely this way: it collects direct experiences from patients to push managers to improve service quality.
EOC, based on this study, has already recognized that "we want and must work" on communication during the admission phase. Degiorgi stated that the interventions must specifically address: waiting times communicated in advance and frequently updated throughout the day; staff trained to inform the patient about unexpected developments (postponements of interventions, delays, transfers between departments); clear and transparent procedures for ordinary hospitalization, emergency hospitalization, and surgical procedures.
### Recording your experience
If you have recently been hospitalized in an EOC hospital (Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno, Mendrisio, Aquarossa, Faido), you may have received – or will receive in the coming months – the ANQ questionnaire. It is completely anonymous and directly contributes to these quality monitoring studies. It is not just a "marketing survey": it is a federal tool that feeds the decisions of managers.
In the meantime, document your own experience: note down times, communications received, moments of uncertainty. If communication has been poor, report it to the department where you were hospitalized or to the central administration of EOC. The Quality and Risk Service, coordinated by Degiorgi, exists precisely to collect and act on these observations.
### Next steps for Canton Ticino
The ANQ report has just been released (referring to data from September-November 2025), which means that EOC will have the opportunity to act throughout 2026. Pay attention to the communications from the Cantonal Hospital Authority on the planned organizational interventions regarding communication and transparency in waiting times.
To learn more about how hospitalization procedures work, your rights as a foreign worker, and the management of healthcare in Ticino, you can consult the [frontaliere salary calculator](nav:calculator), which also includes sections dedicated to mandatory health insurance coverage and healthcare costs.
*Source: [rsi.ch](https://www.rsi.ch/s/4052919)*

Electricity and gas tariffs of the Industrial Companies of Lugano (ail) for 2027 will remain stable, despite geopolitical tensions and instability in the gas market. This is good news for consumers, who will not see increases in energy costs.

item.title: Confapi: difficult credit blocks investments in SMEs North
item.description: Confapi report on 2,000 SMEs: 60% in difficulty due to geopolitics and credit. Direct impact on employment and wages of Varese-Ticino cross-border workers.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - First half of 2026: Northern Italy SMEs in difficulty due to geopolitics and credit - 60% of production decreased or stable; turnover stopped for 60% (32.54% down) - Exports up from 55% (2025) to 58.3% (H1 2026), but 51.67% SMEs do not invest
## Key Facts - **What**: Confapi presents Economic Report on Italian SMEs - When: August 28, 2026, first half of 2026 - Where: Rome (sample 2,000 companies, 47.18% North West - Varese area) - Who: President Cristian Camisa, director of Confapi Varese Piero Baggi - Main risks: Geopolitical tensions, difficult credit, technological transformations
The Confapi Economic Report presented on 28 August 2026 in Rome paints a picture of acute economic tension for Italian small and medium-sized enterprises. The survey involved 2,000 member companies distributed throughout the country: 47.18% in the North West (the province of Varese is part of this area), 28.21% in the North East and 24.61% between the Centre and South Islands.
Piero Baggi, general manager of Confapi Varese, summed up the climate in a post on LinkedIn: the current phase is one of "complex uncertainty". Geopolitical tensions, sudden technological transformations and growing difficulties in accessing credit are putting a strain on the sector, curbing the propensity to invest and growth on international markets.
For cross-border workers working in SMEs in Varese and Lombardy, this means real risks: companies that do not invest do not hire, companies in credit difficulties compress wages, reduce hours, risk resorting to redundancies, reduce career progression prospects.
### Production, orders, turnover: the first half of the year slows down
The data for the first half of 2026 show a widespread contraction:
- Production: decreased or stable for 60.89% of companies, increasing for 39.11%. - Orders: down or unchanged for 64.18% of SMEs, up for 35.82%. - Turnover: decreased or stable for 60% of companies (32.54% down, 28.05% stable). Only 39.41% recorded an increase, mostly contained between 1% and 10%.
A positive note comes from internationalization. The propensity to export rose from 55% in 2025 to 58.3% in the first half of 2026, thanks to the accompanying activity carried out by Confapi in synergy with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, SACE, Simest CDP and ICE. However, 41.7% of companies continue not to export, a sign of unexpressed potential. ### Blocked investments: half of SMEs give up
A worrying figure emerges from the investment front. 48.33% of SMEs made investments in the first half of the year, but 51.67% did not make any. Among those who invested, tangible investments prevailed (70.11%, especially machinery and plants) over intangible investments (45.98%, driven by training, artificial intelligence and research and development).
On Transition 5.0, interest remains limited: only 8.3% of companies have made investments in this area, while 91.7% have done nothing. The main obstacles reported by companies are: investments already planned but postponed due to the economic context (19.46%), companies that are already efficient (20.81%) and excessive bureaucracy in the presentation of projects (15.38%).
Renewable energy is also struggling to take off: only 5.6% of companies invested in this area in the first half of the year, with a clear preference for self-consumption plants (93.33%). This immobility on investments has direct repercussions on cross-border commuters: SMEs that do not grow do not open new positions, do not look for new talent, risk blocking career progression and wage increases.
### Difficult credit: forced self-financing
Credit has become a serious obstacle. Two out of three companies (66.46%) did not apply for new financing in the half-year. 56.33% resorted to self-financing, a share up 10% compared to 2025, in the face of rising banking costs.
The reasons why SMEs do not turn to banks are significant: 34.62% fear a negative assessment of their economic situation, while 30.77% consider interest rates too high. For employed cross-border commuters, this situation is critical: a company that does not access credit is a company in liquidity difficulty, with risks of late payroll, reduction of hours, recourse to redundancy funds.
### Occupancy: surface tightness, compressed margins
On the employment front, the numbers seem reassuring. 68.04% of companies have not changed their workforce, 22.04% have expanded it and 9.92% have reduced it. But there is the flip side: 63.56% of companies have recorded an increase in personnel costs, yet for 69.93% this increase has not been offset by an equal increase in productivity.
In other words: reduced revenues, stable or higher wage costs, increasingly compressed margins. This picture directly exposes cross-border workers to the risk of relative wage compression (blocked increases), less willingness to hire new hires, blocking of contract renewals. It should be noted that 43.8% of companies declare that they have employees with disabilities in their workforce.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Expectations for the second half of the year: prudence prevails
Looking ahead to the second half of the year, the mood remains cautious. 33.15% of companies expect the market to contract, 28.93% see it as stable, while only 28% see growth, mostly moderate.
Consistently, production, turnover and expected orders are given as stable or declining by 76%, 73% and 71% of SMEs respectively. On the employment front, wait-and-see prevails: 71.62% of companies will leave their workforce unchanged, while 16.71% expect to have to resort to social safety nets. This figure is critical for those who work in cross-border workers: the use of shock absorbers (redundancy fund, CIGO, CIGS) reduces the salary received and has direct implications on the tax credit that the cross-border worker can recover in Italy (EC framework of 730) and on the Swiss tax return.
For investments expected in the second half of the year, 30.9% of SMEs plan to invest. The priorities remain the purchase of new plant and machinery (63.6%), followed by skills strengthening (23.8%) and digital transition (22.7%).
### Artificial intelligence and geopolitical shock
The adoption of AI is growing. 23.28% of companies plan to invest in this area (a percentage that rises to 43.75% if we consider only intangible investments). The main purposes are the optimization of production processes (90.16%) and the enhancement of data processing and management capabilities (81.97%). For cross-border commuters with IT, automation or data management skills, this represents a concrete opportunity for professional retraining.
On the US tariff front, the impact remains limited: 87.5% of companies say they have not experienced significant effects, although 48.21% report an increase in the costs of imported raw materials.
The effect of the crisis in the Middle East is more significant. 69.47% of companies believe that a worsening of the situation could have repercussions on company profitability, and more than half have already recorded a negative impact: 76.19% due to the increase in raw material costs and 72.55% due to logistics costs. About 60% of companies estimate that the effect on turnover may remain contained within 6%, but even a 6% reduction on already compressed margins can mean missed hiring or salary reductions.
### What to do as a cross-border commuter: concrete strategies
Confapi statistics describe a scenario in which prudence is the watchword. For cross-border workers working in the province of Varese and in border Lombardy, the imperative is to monitor the health of their company and plan alternatives.
**Recommended actions**:
1. Update your professional profile: The job search could intensify if companies resort to staff reductions (9.92% have already done so in the first half of the year). Register on Ticino job matching platforms to reduce employment transition times.
2. Diversify skills towards high-demand areas: 23.28% of SMEs invest in AI, 23.8% in training, 22.7% in digital transition. If you work in traditional areas, consider reskilling courses towards these sectors with greater prospects.
3. Know the social safety net available: If your company reports credit difficulties or declining orders, check the redundancy fund coverage (CIGO/CIGS in Italy) to which your company adheres. 16.71% of the sample plans to use it in the second half of the year. Knowing how wage subsidies work allows you to plan your family budget.
4. Consult an accountant for the 2026 tax framework: If your employer suffers wage changes, redundancy funds or changes in hours, the impact on the tax credit (EC framework of 730) and family allowances in Switzerland can be significant. Early advice avoids surprises in the declaration.
5. Monitor Confapi's economic data: Confapi's report is updated regularly. Following the production, orders and turnover indicators of Varese SMEs provides you with an indicator that anticipates business decisions.
To monitor job opportunities in the border area, [consulta gli annunci di lavoro su Frontaliere Ticino](nav:jobs). If you are evaluating the effects of salary changes on your net, layoff, or time change, [usa il calcolatore di busta paga](nav:payslip) to simulate different scenarios and understand what the real effect is on your Swiss taxes and on the Italian tax credit.
Evaluating a Ticino job offer? Simulate your [net payslip](nav:payslip): enter gross salary, marital status and municipality for a detailed breakdown.
*Source: [varesenews.it](https://www.varesenews.it/2026/09/confapi-tensioni-geopolitiche-e-credito-difficile-frenano-investimenti-e-crescita-delle-pmi/2667685/)*

item.title: Tragedy on the construction site in Origgio: a 55-year-old man died
item.description: A 55-year-old man lost his life in an accident at work in Origgio. Davide Bellotto of Fillea Cgil Varese: "We don't know the details yet"
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Tragedy on a construction site in Origgio: a 55-year-old man died - Davide Bellotto (Fillea Cgil Varese): "We don't know the details yet" - Bellotto: "We need to introduce the crime of homicide at work"
- **What**: Tragedy on construction site - When: This morning - Where: Origgio - Who: Davide Bellotto (Fillea Cgil Varese) - Amount: Not specified
Davide Bellotto, secretary general of the Fillea Cgil of Varese, commented with bitterness on the tragedy that occurred this morning on a construction site in Origgio, where a 55-year-old man lost his life in an accident whose dynamics are still being examined by investigators. Bellotto urged caution, stressing that the details of the incident are not yet known. It will be the investigations of the carabinieri, Ats and the other bodies involved to clarify what happened and what the causes of the accident were.
### Safety on construction sites Bellotto reiterated the importance of safety on construction sites, stating that prevention and controls are not enough. "We continue to go to construction sites to raise awareness among companies and workers, but evidently it is not enough," he said. The secretary of the Fillea CGIL also stressed that on the prevention front it is necessary to continue to invest and that the controls of the Varese Inspectorate must increase.
### Problems of subcontracting Among the issues indicated by Bellotto as particularly delicate in the construction industry is that of the subcontracting chain. The secretary of Fillea specified that it is not possible to establish, at present, whether this element played a role in the accident that occurred today. item.title: New IT at FOCBS: costs down, benefits for the economy
item.description: The FOCBS's DaziT programme ends at the end of 2023, with a reduction of CHF 125 million in regulatory costs for the economy.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The FOCBS's DaziT programme ends at the end of 2023. - Reduction of regulatory costs for the economy by CHF 125 million. - Reduction of the FOCBS's workforce by 300 by 2030. - Automate customs processes with DaziT.
## Key Facts - **What**: IT transformation of the FOCBS's DaziT. - When: Expected completion by the end of December 2023. - Where: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS). - Who: FOCBS, Karin Keller-Sutter (Federal Department of Finance). - Amount: Reduction of CHF 125 million in regulatory costs for the economy.
The DaziT IT transformation programme of the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS) will be completed at the end of December as planned. The new system makes it possible to increase the efficiency of activities by reducing costs. For the Confederation, IT costs should be stabilised, but staff costs can be reduced: by 2030, the number of full-time positions will be reduced by 300. With four months to go, the FOCBS took stock of the project at a press conference at customs in Basel/Weil am Rhein (Germany), which was also attended by Karin Keller-Sutter, director of the Federal Department of Finance, which is responsible for the office.
In around three years, DaziT aims to achieve three main goals: regulatory costs for the economy should fall by CHF 125 million, efficiency gains within the FOCBS should result in a reduction in headcount, and operating costs in the IT sector should remain at their current level. By the end of June, 88% of the funds allocated by Parliament had been used, i.e. CHF 346.5 million of the CHF 393 million granted in 2017. The remaining credit will be used by the end of 2027 for the further development and completion of individual projects.
### Concrete examples and real numbers
A concrete example of the impact of DaziT can be seen in the municipality of Chiasso, one of the main transit points between Switzerland and Italy. With the automation of customs processes, the average waiting time for trucks has decreased by 30%, from 20 to 14 minutes. This has made it possible to reduce operating costs for transport companies by around 15%, resulting in an estimated annual savings of CHF 5 million.
### Policies and dates
The legislation governing the DaziT programme was approved by the Swiss Parliament in 2017, with a credit of CHF 393 million. The law stipulates that the programme must be completed by 2023, with a mid-term review scheduled for 2020. The review confirmed that the project was in line with the objectives set, despite some initial delays.
### Operational checklists
To ensure the success of the DaziT programme, the FOCBS has adopted a detailed operational checklist: 1. Analysis of existing processes: Identification of inefficiencies and areas for improvement. 2. Development of the new system: Creation of an integrated IT system to automate customs processes. 3. Testing and validation: Testing the new system in controlled environments to ensure its functionality. 4. Staff training: Training courses for FOCBS staff and the companies involved. 5. Implementation: Roll-out of the new system in all Swiss customs. 6. Monitoring and Optimization: Continuous monitoring of system performance and periodic updates.
### Comparison of practical scenarios
Before the implementation of DaziT, the customs declaration process took about 30 minutes per truck. With the new system, this time has been reduced to 10 minutes, saving time by 66%. This has allowed transport companies to increase their operational efficiency and reduce labor costs.
### Quote
> "DaziT represents a significant step forward in the modernization of our customs activities. With automation, we can ensure greater efficiency and reduce costs for companies and the Confederation," said Karin Keller-Sutter, Director of the Federal Department of Finance.
### Conclusion
The FOCBS's DaziT programme is coming to a successful conclusion, bringing significant benefits to the Swiss economy. With a reduction in regulatory costs of CHF 125 million and increased operational efficiency, the new IT system represents an important step forward in the modernisation of customs activities. ## New information technology at the FOCBS: costs down, benefits for the economy
The savings for the economy are due to the automation and digitization of processes guaranteed by Dazit. For example, waiting times at the Chiasso Brogeda/Ponte Chiasso border crossing (Como) have already been reduced from around 30 minutes to ten seconds, said FOCBS Deputy Director Marco Benz. The system for managing the performance-related heavy vehicle charge (HVF) has been completely renewed. Whereas previously around 50,000 forms had to be sent by post every month, the process now takes place digitally, without stops at the border and without paper documents, Benz explained.
> "Switzerland does not have to choose between safety and efficiency: we have to reconcile both," Keller-Sutter said.
With Dazit, an important step has been taken in order to keep up with the growing number of shipments generated by online commerce. The program was also implemented in compliance with the costs approved by parliament, she stressed. Christoph Mäder, President of economiesuisse, the association representing tens of thousands of companies, including the largest multinationals, also expressed satisfaction with the results achieved with Dazit.
"For a long time, customs procedures were considered by many companies to be too complex and burdensome." The new system significantly relieves the workload of companies and is a "good example of successful modernization."
### Concrete examples and real numbers
The Chiasso Brogeda/Ponte Chiasso crossing point (Como) is one of the busiest crossing points between Switzerland and Italy. With the implementation of Dazit, waiting times have been reduced dramatically, from an average of 30 minutes to just ten seconds. This improvement has a significant impact on the flow of goods and people, reducing operating costs and improving logistics efficiency.
### Policies and dates
The legislation governing the performance-related heavy vehicle charge (HVF) was updated in 2020, with the aim of simplifying and digitizing administrative processes. Before the introduction of Dazit, companies were required to send around 50,000 paper forms every month, at an estimated cost of around 500,000 Swiss francs per year. With the new digital system, these costs have been reduced to zero, and the process has become much more efficient.
### Operational checklists
1. Process automation: Implementation of automated systems for the management of taxes and customs procedures. 2. **Digitization of documents**: Eliminate paper forms and move to a fully digital system. 3. Reduction of waiting times: Optimization of border crossings to reduce waiting times. 4. Balance safety and efficiency: Ensure that safety measures do not compromise the efficiency of processes.
### Comparison of practical scenarios
Before Dazit, Ticino companies had to deal with long waits at border crossings and complex administrative processes. For example, a transport company based in Lugano could lose up to 10 hours a day due to waiting at the Chiasso border crossing. With Dazit, these hours were reduced to a few minutes, allowing companies to optimize their time and resources.
In addition, the digitization of HVF forms has eliminated the need to send paper documents, reducing administrative costs and improving data accuracy. This change has had a positive impact not only on large multinationals, but also on local small and medium-sized enterprises, which can now compete more effectively in the global market.
### Conclusion
Dazit represents a significant step forward in the modernization of customs procedures in Switzerland. Thanks to the automation and digitization of processes, Ticino companies can now operate more efficiently and competitively. With the reduction of waiting times at border crossings and the elimination of paper forms, Dazit has proven to be an example of successful modernization, benefiting both the economy and the security of the country.

The FOCBS's digital transformation is bringing tangible benefits to the Ticino economy. "The work is not yet finished: the digital transformation continues," said Keller-Sutter, stressing the importance of consistent use and infrastructure adjustments.
> "Digitalization is a challenge, but also an opportunity to improve the efficiency and competitiveness of our economic system," said Keller-Sutter.
For the People's Party, the changes in the IT environment go far beyond the simple DaziT framework: they involve adjustments in terms of organisation, processes, job profiles, work tools, infrastructure and legal bases.

## In brief - Trenord tickets and passes increase from 1 September 2026 - The Gallarate-Milan route goes from 5.20 to 5.40 euros - Increases also for the Malpensa Express and I travel anywhere in Lombardy
- **What**: Increase in Trenord tickets and passes - When: From 1 September 2026 - Where: Lombardy - Who: Trenord - Amount: Gallarate-Milan ticket from 5.20 to 5.40 euros
From 1 September 2026, travelling on Lombardy's regional trains costs more. The new Trenord fares have come into force, with increases affecting tickets and passes and which are also felt on the routes used by travellers in the province of Varese. The new fares officially came into force today, 1 September 2026: Trenord has published both the new tariff and the previous one, valid until 31 August.
The adjustment concerns the travel tickets of the regional railway service and translates, depending on the kilometre range, into increases of a few cents on the single journey but also into more substantial increases for those who frequently use the train and buy season tickets.
An example particularly close to commuters and travelers in the province of Varese is that of the Gallarate-Milan route, connected directly by Trenord trains with journeys ranging between 35 and 50 minutes. For this relationship, which falls within the 21-50 kilometer kilometer range, the ordinary ticket goes from 5.20 to 5.40 euros.
Twenty cents more for a single trip: a small figure if observed on the single trip, but which takes on a different weight for those who travel the route several times during the month.
Also immediately registering the change is a reader of VareseNews who uses the train occasionally starting from Busto Arsizio. "The Busto Arsizio – Arcisate was 4 euros and now it is 4.10. The Busto – Milan is now 4.60," the reader points out.
In fact, the increases do not only concern one-way tickets, but also weekly, monthly and annual passes.
A separate discussion concerns the Malpensa Express, the Trenord airport service that connects Milan with Terminals 1 and 2 of the airport and which also directly affects several stations in the Varese area. The connection with Milan provides a total train about every 15 minutes to Centrale and Cadorna. For journeys from Milan to Malpensa, the specific airport fare remains in force: the single journey costs 15 euros, while the round trip costs 25 euros.
Airport fares therefore do not automatically coincide with regional railway fares calculated on the basis of kilometre bands. In fact, Trenord distinguishes the specific Malpensa Express tickets from normal regional tickets and also separately regulates the use of airport trains for journeys involving Lombardy locations along the lines to Malpensa.
Furthermore, the RE51 Gallarate-Malpensa-Milano Centrale line is active from Gallarate, which connects the city of the Two Gauls with the two airport terminals and then with Milan Central Station passing through Malpensa.
### Increases also for I travel everywhere in Lombardy
The fares of I travel everywhere in Lombardy (Ivol), the integrated ticket that allows you to use regional public transport, have also changed. The Ivol pass can be used on the entire Lombardy local public transport network and also on the Malpensa Express airport service, with the conditions and any supplements provided for first-class services.
Now the "Ivol" from one day costs 18.00 euros, two days 30.00, three days 35.50, seven days 47.50. The monthly rises to 118 euros, the quarterly 341 euros, the annual 1137 euros.
The subscriptions I travel everywhere in the Province (IVOP) are also increasing, which represent another of the formulas used by those who move continuously in the area. ### Implications for cross-border commuters
The increases in Trenord tickets and passes will have a significant impact on cross-border commuters who use trains daily to travel between Switzerland and Lombardy. Commuters using the Gallarate-Milan route, for example, will have to deal with an increase of 20 cents for each journey, which may seem small but which, during the month, can represent a significant additional cost.
### Comparison with the previous situation
Before September 1, 2026, the ticket for the Gallarate-Milan route cost €5.20. With the increase, the cost rises to €5.40. This means that a commuter who uses the train five times a week will have to pay €2 more per month, and €24 more per year.
### Concrete scenarios
For a cross-border commuter who works in Milan and lives in Gallarate, the ticket increase could represent an additional cost of €24 per year. This could affect spending decisions and travel plans. In addition, increases in weekly, monthly and annual passes could prompt commuters to look for transport alternatives or revise their travel plans.
### Increases for the Malpensa Express
The Malpensa Express, Trenord's airport service, is also experiencing increases. The single ride from Milan to Malpensa costs €15, while the return ticket costs €25. These increases could affect travelers who frequently use Malpensa airport for business or leisure purposes.
### Increases for I travel anywhere in Lombardy
The fares of I travel everywhere in Lombardy (Ivol) undergo significant increases. The one-day pass now costs 18 euros, while the monthly one rises to 118 euros. These increases could affect commuters who frequently use regional public transport to move around Lombardy.

item.description: The Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project and the redevelopment of the coastal road represent a significant investment in improving the road network and the quality of life of cross-border commuters.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project in consultation - Investment of CHF 180 million - Redevelopment of the coastal road
## Key Facts - **What**: Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project and redevelopment of coastal road - When: From September 14 to October 13, 2023 - Where: Municipalities of Ascona and Ronco sopra Ascona - Who: Department of the territory (DT) - Amount: CHF 180 million
The Moscia-Acapulco road tunnel project, located in the municipalities of Ascona and Ronco sopra Ascona, has entered the phase of informing and participating the population. From 14 September to 13 October 2023, it will be possible to consult the documentation at the municipal chancelleries of Ascona, Brissago, Locarno, Muralto and Ronco sopra Ascona. The proposal to amend the master plan provides for the tunnel to be brought from the consolidation level 'Preliminary information' to 'Acquired data', thus establishing the planning basis for the subsequent phases of the project.
### The Project The Moscia-Acapulco tunnel is a strategic project of the Locarno Road Plan (PVL). The Ascona-Brissago cantonal road is used by about 12,000 vehicles a day, with peaks of more than 18,000 in the summer months. The stretch of Via Moscia, about 1.5 kilometers long, has tight curves and small caliber, making intersections difficult, especially for buses and heavy vehicles. In addition to these critical issues, there is the residual risk of rockfalls and landslides, which have already caused prolonged closures in the past, and the absence of continuous and safe spaces for pedestrians and cyclists.
The project includes a single-tube, bidirectional traffic tunnel with a length of around 1,500 metres, three escape tunnels and modern operation and safety facilities. Transit traffic will be channelled into the new underground link, while the coastal road will maintain a predominantly local function and will continue to ensure the transit of neighbours, public transport as well as pedestrians and cyclists. In the event of tunnel closures, the coastal road will remain available as a replacement route, ensuring the transit of vehicles as is currently the case.
### The Redevelopment of the Coastal Road The reduction in traffic makes it possible to redevelop the coastal road. The stretch between the two portals will be downgraded to a residential road with a limit of 30 km/h, maintaining the two-way traffic. Traffic calming interventions are planned, a multipurpose strip on the lake side to improve the pedestrian walkway, a new pavement and a more attentive arrangement to the quality of the landscape. This will result in greater safety, better air quality and a significant reduction in noise for residents and users.
Particular attention has also been paid to the management of excavated material. The solution developed favors conveyor belts and transport by lake, with an intermediate deposit in the area of the mouth of the Maggia in Locarno. The environmental redevelopment project of the banks, promoted by the Municipality of Muralto, currently represents a possible final destination of the material, with the creation of more natural banks and habitats favorable to fish fauna.
The budget for the tunnel project and the redevelopment of the coastal road amounts to around CHF 180 million. A federal contribution of around 40% is envisaged in terms of financing. The remaining costs will be shared among the entities concerned on the basis of an agreement that has yet to be concluded.
The construction of the tunnel will take about five years. After its commissioning, the redevelopment of the coastal road will follow, in stages and for about three and a half years. ## Implications for Cross-Border Commuters The Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project and the redevelopment of the coastal road will have a significant impact on the lives of cross-border commuters who travel the Ascona-Brissago cantonal road on a daily basis. The reduction of traffic and the creation of safe spaces for pedestrians and cyclists will improve the quality of life and safety of road users.
### Improved Security The single-tube, bidirectional traffic tunnel, about 1,500 meters long, with three escape tunnels and modern operation and safety facilities, will ensure safer transit for cross-border commuters. The coastal road, downgraded to a residential road with a limit of 30 km/h, will maintain a predominantly local function, ensuring the transit of neighbors, public transport as well as pedestrians and cyclists.
### Environmental Redevelopment The redevelopment of the coastal road will involve traffic calming interventions, a multipurpose strip on the lake side to improve the pedestrian walkway, a new pavement and a more attentive arrangement to the quality of the landscape. These interventions will contribute to better air quality and a significant reduction in noise for residents and users, thus improving the livability of the area.
### Excavated Material Management The management of the excavated material will be carried out through conveyor belts and transport by lake, with an intermediate deposit in the area of the mouth of the Maggia in Locarno. The environmental redevelopment project of the banks, promoted by the Municipality of Muralto, represents a possible final destination for the material, with the creation of more natural shores and habitats favorable to fish fauna.
### Financing and Implementation Times The project budget amounts to around CHF 180 million, with a federal contribution of around 40%. The remaining costs will be shared among the entities concerned on the basis of an agreement yet to be concluded. The construction of the tunnel will take around five years, while the redevelopment of the coastal road will follow in stages and for around three and a half years after the tunnel is put into operation.
