item.title: Living in Villette and working in Ticino as a border worker
item.description: Living in Villette as a cross-border commuter and working in Ticino: transport, costs and tax advantages. Guide to crossings, AHV regulations, G Permit and administrative deadlines.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Villette is an ideal border area for those who work in Ticino - Fast transport from the Chiasso and Brogeda passes to Lugano/Mendrisio - Lower housing costs, advantageous cross-border taxation from 2024 - Mandatory G permit, AHV/BVG/KG regulations in force from 1 January 2024
## Key Facts - **Where**: Villette, municipality in the province of Como, Lombardy — Ticino border - Who: Cross-border commuters category G under transitional regime or new 2024+ agreement - What: Living in a residential area, working in Ticino - When: New Cross-Border Commuters Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Permit: Mandatory G permit for cross-border workers - Taxation: Withholding tax only in Switzerland; double taxation avoided via IRPEF credit (EC 730 framework) - Transport: Chiasso/Brogeda passes reached in about 20-40 minutes from Villette
Living in Villette as a cross-border commuter means choosing a quiet residential reality, well connected to the main centers of Ticino through the Chiasso and Brogeda crossings. The small town in the province of Como attracts more and more workers who prefer the lower cost of living compared to Ticino prices, while maintaining direct access to the Swiss labor market.
As of 1 January 2024, the New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement has significantly changed the rules for those who live in Villette and work in Ticino. Cross-border commuters who were already cross-border commuters before 17 July 2023 benefit from a transitional regime with tax exemption of up to CHF 7,500 in income, while new cross-border commuters access a deductible of CHF 10,000. This measure makes the move to Villette even more tax-friendly. In your [dichiarazione dei redditi](nav:tax-return), you will bring the Swiss withholding tax credit back into the EC framework to avoid double taxation.
### The geographical choice: proximity and accessibility
Villette represents the ideal confluence between the Lombard residential market and the reachability of Ticino. The Chiasso and Brogeda passes are accessible in about 20-40 minutes depending on the work destination (Mendrisio, Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno). The state road 13 and the A2 motorway towards the Gotthard pass nearby, making daily mobility predictable.
For those who work in Lugano or in the municipalities of the Sottocentesi, the route usually includes the Brogeda or Chiasso pass; for the Mendrisiotto (Mendrisio, Balerna), Chiasso is the fastest choice. Travel times depend on the exact point of work in Ticino and traffic conditions, but the Villette area is undoubtedly among the most convenient for commuting to Ticino.
### G permit and residency: what not to miss
To live legally in Villette and work in Ticino, the G Permit (cross-border commuter) is mandatory. It is not a simple documentation: it is the legal prerequisite for withholding tax in Switzerland and for access to the rules of AHV (old age insurance), [LPP](nav:pension) (occupational pension) and KVG (health insurance).
The G Permit is requested from the Prefecture (or Provincial Government Office) of Como and must be renewed annually. The typical duration of the procedure is 1-2 months. KVG health insurance in Switzerland is compulsory for cross-border commuters: adult deductibles start at CHF 300 per year and Swiss companies cover 50% of the premium. ### Concrete border taxation: how the withholding tax works
Those who work in Ticino as cross-border commuters with a G permit are subject to withholding tax only in Switzerland. Italy recognizes the tax credit: the withholding tax paid in Switzerland is reported in the EC framework of the tax return, avoiding double taxation. The tax rate varies by canton and income; in Ticino it is around 15-18% (federal + cantonal).
The tax base discounts the deductibles of the New Agreement: CHF 7,500 for old cross-border commuters (transitional regime 2024-2033) or CHF 10,000 for new ones. Example: an annual salary of CHF 60,000, for an already registered cross-border commuter, is taxed on CHF 52,500. At a rate of 15%, the withholding tax is about CHF 7,875, which becomes a tax credit in the Italian IRPEF return.
### Contributions and payroll: AHV, BVG, net calculation
Since 1 January 2024, cross-border commuters category G have been paying AHV/IV contributions of 5.3% in Switzerland (employee share) and BVG occupational pension provision of 7-18% per age group. In addition, unemployment insurance (ALV) is 1.1% up to CHF 148,200, and UVG accident 0.7%-1.5%.
On a gross salary of CHF 4,500 per month, the total withholdings (AHV, ALV, UVG, BVG, withholding tax) amount to around CHF 800-950 per month. The expected monthly net is CHF 2,550-2,700, which varies by canton and family composition. For cross-border commuters from Villette, the net in CHF corresponds to EUR 2,350-2,500 at the average exchange rate (CHF 1 ≈ EUR 0.92-0.96). ### Transfer procedure: step-by-step
Step 1 - Before moving: Check the availability of work in Ticino with a signed offer. Contact the Prefecture of Como for the time to apply for Permit G; usually 1-2 months.
Step 2 - Acquire the G Permit: Apply to the Prefecture accompanied by a Swiss employment contract, declaration from the Swiss employer, identity document, Italian certificate of residence. The G Permit is valid for 12 months and must be renewed every year.
Step 3 - Administrative communications: Once the G Permit has been obtained, the cross-border commuter must notify the change in employment situation to the Italian Revenue Agency (form AA9/12, which notifies INPS). In addition, inform the employer of any changes in residence or family members that affect Swiss AHV/taxation.
Step 4 - Open bank account and currency transfers: Many cross-border commuters from Villette open a Swiss bank account (Ticino) for CHF salary and an Italian one for EUR recurring accounts. The CHF/EUR exchange rate varies daily; it is advisable to monitor it and make transfers when the exchange rate is favorable.
### Checklists and annual deadlines
- January: Check the update of the G Permit for the current year. - March-April: Italian IRPEF declaration (form 730 or PF Income with CE framework) at the Revenue Agency. - June: Review of health insurance coverage (KVG or CMI). - November-December: Planning of the Swiss third pillar 3a (payment by 31 December for Swiss tax deductibility).
### Evaluate costs and benefits before moving
Living in Villette has advantages (housing costs generally lower than in the Canton of Ticino, geographical proximity, border taxation with deductibles) and disadvantages (daily commuting, double tax administration, transport/petrol costs). We recommend simulating the expected monthly net CHF after all withholdings and comparing it with the costs of rent, utilities and transport in Villette vs alternative of living in Ticino.
Use our [calcolatore fiscale frontalieri](nav:calculator) to estimate the precise monthly net according to your situation (salary, cross-border commuter category, canton of Ticino, marital status). You will have a realistic picture of the net gain and can make an informed decision whether the transfer is worthwhile economically.

item.title: Evaluating the Return of Training: 2026 How-To Guide
item.description: How to assess whether training is worthwhile: practical checklist, simulation scenarios and decision-making criteria for cross-border commuters in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Assessing the opportunity cost of training before investing is critical for cross-border commuters - A practical checklist helps you compare available courses and funding - ROI simulation estimates how long it takes to amortize the investment - Alternative scenarios show the career differential at 2-5 years
## Key Facts - **What**: Methodology for evaluating the practical return of a vocational training - When: Assessment to be carried out before enrolling in a course - Where: Relevant for cross-border commuters working in Switzerland or considering CH opportunities - Who: Cross-border commuters in career transition, with the need for retraining or professional upgrade - Duration: Simulation covers a span of 2-5 years post-training - Tool: Payroll calculator to quantify the tax impact of the wage increase
Vocational education and training is one of the most important investments in a cross-border commuter's career. Unlike purely personal choices, a training decision has a direct impact on gross salary, qualifications recognised in Switzerland and cross-border employment prospects. However, many cross-border commuters do not have a systematic tool to assess whether a specific course is really worthwhile, considering time lost from work, direct costs and alternative opportunities.
2026 represents a critical year for those considering retraining: the Ticino and Swiss labor markets are evolving, some sectors require new skills, and public funding for continuing education remains available in specific ways for those who cross the border on a daily basis.
### Why evaluate before investing
Investing time and money in training without having a clear vision of the return on investment (ROI) exposes the cross-border commuter to concrete risks: prolonged amortization of costs, qualifications that are not directly expendable on the Swiss market, conflicts with current working hours. A structured evaluation makes it possible to distinguish between courses that offer real employment value and those that remain episodic in the curriculum. ## Practical Assessment Methodology
The first step is to map out the measurable elements of each course: duration (hours/months), direct cost (tuition, materials, software), opportunity cost (lost work days or reduced salary), and the expected earnings differential over time. Not all courses generate immediate salary increases; some provide certifications that enable you to new roles after 6-18 months.
The second step is to compare the value of the certification obtained with the local and Swiss market. A certification recognized by the Federal Office of Vocational Education and Training (FOPH) or by cantonal bodies has structural value; a private certification, even a quality one, may require further validation at the time of job placement.
### Decision criteria checklist
Before you sign up, answer these key questions:
Consistency with the career project Is this skill in demand by employers in your industry? Does it shift your profile to better-paying or more stable roles? Is it consistent with your current trajectory, or does it represent a radical pivot?
**Economic sustainability** Can you cover the tuition without resorting to high-interest loans? How many days of work will you lose, and how much is this loss worth economically? Are there public funding, employer bonuses or exchanges for which you are eligible?
Recognizability and credibility Is the training provider accredited at federal, cantonal or EU level? Are the skills acquired certified transparently (diplomas, badges, verifiable certificates)? Are they transferable between sectors or are they too specific to an employer?
Timing and Flexibility Can you take the course without compromising your current working hours or family situation? If your return is lower than expected, can you recover quickly without lasting effects?
Once this information has been gathered, the practical simulation can begin. The next step is to actually quantify the expected financial return.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Step-by-step simulation of the return
The practical simulation follows a simple but robust model: it estimates the total cost of the investment, projects the additional annual post-training gain, calculates the payback period (years needed to recoup the investment), and compares this scenario with the alternative of not training.
Step 1: Calculate the total cost of training Tuition sum, books, software, supplementary online courses. Add opportunity cost: (training days) × (current daily wage) or a percentage reduction in salary if you take the course in parallel. Total = Direct Cost + Opportunity Cost.
Step 2: Estimate the additional annual earnings Research the average salary for professionals with your new qualification in the Ticino/Swiss market (don't be based on assumptions). Subtract your current (gross) salary. This is the potential gross increase. It is NOT immediate; it could occur in 6-24 months after completion.
Step 3: Estimate the payback period Divide the Total Cost by the Gross Annual Increase. Hypothetical example (generic numbers): Cost CHF 12,000, Increase CHF 3,000 per year → Payback = 4 years. If the payback exceeds 5-6 years, think critically: the course is only worthwhile if it offers other advantages (stability, long-term planning, access to unreachable sectors without qualification).
**Step 4: Compare scenarios** Scenario A: You do not take the course. Stable salary for the next 5 years (projection with inflation and standard contract adjustments). Scenario B: Take the course now. You incur the cost, but you earn the estimated increase starting from month 6/12 post-training. 5-year net spread = (Scenario B - Total cost) - Scenario A. If the 5-year spread is positive and significant (>CHF 10,000), the course deserves serious consideration.
### How to use the calculator to refine the estimate
Use the [calcolatore netto della busta paga](nav:payslip) to enter your pre-training and post-training gross income; the system shows how much your new salary impacts your net paycheck and tax burden (withholding tax, AHV/BVG contributions). Remember that Switzerland applies a withholding tax on earned income; a gross increase is not the same as an identical net increase.
Project the net differential over 2, 3 and 5 years to get a realistic view. Also enter your current tax deductions (AHV/IV/EO, BVG CONTRIBUTIONS IF PRESENT IN THE COMPANY, KVG HEALTH INSURANCE), SO THE SIMULATOR TAKES INTO ACCOUNT THE TOTAL SOCIAL SECURITY CONTRIBUTIONS.
Last step: check if the [formazione riduce il rischio di disoccupazione](nav:unemployment) in your industry. Sometimes a certification pushes down the payback period not because it increases wages immediately, but because it stabilizes employment and reduces the risk of layoffs during unfavorable economic cycles.
Consult the funding and calls for cross-border training in the Canton of Ticino to check if you are eligible for subsidies that reduce your direct cost.

item.title: Cross-border retraining 2026: focus on the family
item.description: New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement from 2024: requalification in 2026 net increase and BVG for cross-border commuters with children. Tax analysis and operational checklist.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New Agreement from 1 January 2024: tax benefits for cross-border commuters who retrain - Exemption €7,500 (old) or €10,000 (new) reduces the withholding tax burden - Tax ONLY in Switzerland; Italy avoids double taxation with 730 credit - Cross-border commuters G with children: KVG choice and simplified INPS-AHV coordination
## Key Facts - **What**: Professional retraining with tax benefits aimed at cross-border commuters with children - When: New Agreement effective from 1 January 2024 (signed 23 December 2020) - Where: Work in Ticino (Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano), residence Italy border - Who: Cross-border commuters Permit G; Revenue Agency, AFC/ESTV, INPS, SECO coordinate - Exemption: €7,500 (cross-border commuters from 17 July 2023) or €10,000 (new) - Rates: AHV/IV/EO 5.3%, ALV/CA 1.1%, UVG 0.7–1.5%, BVG 7–18%
The New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement, which came into force on 1 January 2024, redesigns the tax regime for those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy. For cross-border commuters with children who invest in education in 2026, this translates into concrete benefits: withholding tax reductions and simplification of Italian-Swiss coordination.
The key rule: withholding tax is ONLY withheld by Switzerland. Italy avoids double taxation thanks to the tax credit in the 730 form, where the cross-border commuter declares the Swiss net. "Old" cross-border commuters (already such as on 17 July 2023) are entitled to €7,500 annual exemption until 2033; "new" cross-border commuters access €10,000.
Salary in Ticino is subject to compulsory deductions: AHV/IV/EO 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, UVG 0.7–1.5%, BVG 7–18% depending on age. These reductions feed into the Swiss pension (AHV) and the supplementary fund (BVG), which are then coordinated with the Italian INPS for the final calculation of the pension.
### Retraining Scenario: The Net Impact on Payroll
A cross-border commuter who increases his salary by CHF +12,000/year (20% increase) through retraining sees a net increase of around CHF +3,500 per year after taxation, thanks to the exemption. This gain is not eroded by double taxation — the New Agreement guarantees this. At the same time, he accumulates CHF +4,400 in AHV-BVG, which means a higher pension pension at the age of 65.
Dependent children amplify the advantage: the Italian IRPEF grants deductions for each child (about €1,050 each if minors), and the final rebate or adjustment settles in favor of the family.
### Role of the KVG in the redevelopment decision
An often forgotten aspect: the cross-border commuter G permit has [diritto d'opzione tra LAMal svizzera](nav:health) and Italian insurance. With the retraining and increase in income, this choice becomes strategic. If the cross-border commuter opts for KVG Switzerland (with a deductible EUR 300–2,500), the premiums are deducted from the Swiss gross salary — and further reduce the withholding tax. If he stays in Italy (INPS-coordinated insurance with EEA), the premiums are paid separately, but he accesses Italian benefits (maternity, unemployment, family allowances).
The requalification is therefore not just a salary boost, but an opportunity to optimize the insurance mix: LAMal for health protection, LPP for retirement, and INPS coordination for family benefits. The cross-border worker who retrains must update his Italian tax return. The procedure is managed through the 730 model, which has a dedicated section (EC framework) for foreign income.
### The EC declaration: a concrete procedure
1. Obtains salary certificate from Swiss payslip (tax withholding brochure) 2. Converts the SVG net to EUR at the average annual exchange rate of the fiscal year 3. Declares in the EC framework the "income from foreign employment" 4. The Revenue Agency calculates the IRPEF by scaling: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000 5. Apply the tax credit (Swiss withholding tax already paid); if higher than the IRPEF due, the cross-border commuter obtains a refund; otherwise, he pays an adjustment
With the requalification that raises the salary, the IRPEF burden increases nominally, but the tax credit almost always compensates for it — especially if Switzerland has applied progressive rates. The Italy-Switzerland double taxation agreement of 9 December 1976 establishes that if the cross-border worker has paid more tax in Switzerland than he should in Italy, the surplus is refunded as a "refund" within a few months after the submission of the 730.
### Increased income: how double contributions work
A critical aspect of retraining: it increases contributions to BOTH systems. In Switzerland, the employer pays AHV (approx. 5.3% gross), ALV/AC 1.1%, UVG 0.7–1.5%, and the employee pays BVG (7–18% depending on age, from the age of 25 onwards). These contributions build up the Swiss pension pension — the largest part of the future cross-border commuter's pension.
In Italy, on the basis of the income declared in 730, the cross-border worker pays INPS contributions at the end of the year. According to the 1976 Italian-Swiss Convention, those who work in Switzerland pay ONLY AHV (not INPS). However, the coordination between the two systems calculates the final pension as a "weighted sum" of the years in the Swiss system and in the Italian system.
With retraining, the salary increases, AHV contributions increase, and by the time of retirement, the cross-border commuter will have a higher capital accumulated in BVG and a more generous AHV pension.
### Dependent children: the additional deductions that matter
If the cross-border worker has minor children, the Italian IRPEF grants additional deductions: deduction for dependent spouse (about €800), deductions for children (about €1,050 per minor child). These deductions apply directly to the calculated IRPEF and are not proportional to income. This means that if a cross-border commuter with two children has IRPEF of €8,000 gross, family deductions of about €2,100 reduce it to €5,900 net due.
With retraining, income increases (and therefore nominal income tax rises), but the amount of deductions remains stable. As a result, the net gain from retraining is amplified: the family benefits proportionally more than it pays in taxes. This effect is one of the least communicated advantages of the New Cross-Border Worker Agreement for parents. ### Step-by-step checklist: how to concretely proceed in 2026
1. Check your status as a cross-border commuter Check whether you are "old" (already a cross-border commuter on 17 July 2023, €7,500 exemption) or "new" (€10,000 exemption). This info can be found on your SEM Administrative Decision or in the Permit G file. Download the document and keep it handy.
2. Choose the recognized retraining course Federal vocational education and training (apprenticeships, CAS courses, DAS) is automatically admitted. For private courses, check SECO recognition. Document the course: title, duration, provider, start and end date.
3. Simulate the tax impact before signing up Use the [calcolatore di stipendio netto](nav:calculator): enter current gross, estimated post-course increase, number of children → find out your expected net, Swiss withholding tax, Italian rebate/adjustment. Repeat the simulation with the expected final salary.
4. Tell the employer Inform about the course of study and the start date. If the course causes a work break, grant the study permit. If you increase the hours/tasks during the course, the employer must update the salary slip.
5. Gather documents for 730 Swiss pay slips (all months of the tax year), Swiss tax certificate, certificate of attendance of the course, copy of the G permit, possibly certificates of dependent children.
6. Declare new income in 730 By 31 May of the following year, rely on an accountant specialising in cross-border commuters (not all CAFs are familiar with the EC framework). It declares the Swiss net converted into EUR, highlights the tax credit, reports the increase in income due to requalification.
7. Wait for the outcome: rebate or adjustment If the Swiss tax was higher than the Italian tax due, you will receive a refund by bank transfer (usually 3–6 months after submission). If, on the other hand, Italy calculates a debt that is higher than the credit, it pays an adjustment via the F24 form.
### The resources available to learn more
Frontaliere Ticino's [guida al 730 e dichiarazione frontalieri](nav:tax-return) explains the EC framework step by step with examples. To simulate the pension impact of retraining (how much your BVG fund grows), see the [AVS-LPP-INPS e coordinamento](nav:pension) section.
Next step: Use the [calcolatore di stipendio netto](nav:calculator) today to visualize the concrete benefit of your retraining in 2026. If the estimated net is positive, proceed with confidence and contact an accountant specializing in cross-border commuters for the detailed plan of the 730 declaration.

item.title: Chiasso and A2: strengthening and financial challenges
item.description: Chiasso faces complicated projections for the A2 Lugano-Mendrisio upgrade. FEDRO asks the Ticino Executive for accompanying measures. What it means for cross-border commuters.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Chiasso faces 'complicated' financial projections - Concern over the impact of the A2 Lugano-Mendrisio upgrade - Ustra requests accompanying measures from the Executive
## Key facts - **What**: Complicated financial projections for the Municipality of Chiasso - Context: Upgrade of the A2 motorway between Lugano and Mendrisio - Who: Municipality of Chiasso, Ustra (Federal Roads Office), Cantonal Executive - Concern: Impact of the A2 upgrade on the territory - Request: Accompanying measures from Ustra
The Municipality of Chiasso is dealing with complicated financial projections. The main concern is the impact of the upgrade of the A2 motorway, which affects the section between Lugano and Mendrisio. According to the official communication, Ustra (the Swiss Federal Roads Office) is at the table of the Cantonal Executive of Ticino to discuss this strategic issue. The federal agency has requested accompanying measures to mitigate the territorial effects of the motorway upgrade.
The term 'extra muros' in the title seems to refer to the external effects of the structure, i.e., the impact that the A2 project will have on the urban and territorial context of Chiasso.
### The infrastructural context
The A2 motorway represents the main artery connecting Ticino to Italy through the passes, and Chiasso is one of the critical points of crossing for cross-border traffic. The motorway handles the flow of tens of thousands of vehicles per day, including commuters working in northern Switzerland.
The upgrade of the Lugano-Mendrisio section is not just a matter of traffic but also involves financial aspects for the affected municipalities, as infrastructure modifications of this magnitude require compensations and accompanying measures. Monitoring current times at the passes through [official traffic data](nav:traffic-history) helps to better understand how the upgrade could modify future flow.
### What do accompanying measures mean
Ustra has requested accompanying measures from the Cantonal Executive. Although the source does not specify the details, the term 'accompanying' in the context of infrastructure suggests actions aimed at mitigating negative effects (congestion during construction, disturbances to the territory) or maximizing the benefits of the project for the local community.
For commuters who cross Chiasso daily towards Italy, the A2 upgrade represents both opportunities (improved traffic fluidity) and temporary risks (construction phases with possible disruptions). ### How the A2 upgrade affects cross-border commuters
The A2 motorway is the backbone of the Ticino-Italy commute. Chiasso, as the main transit pass, is the point where tens of thousands of cross-border commuters cross daily to Lombardy for work reasons. An expansion of this section has concrete implications for the daily lives of commuters.
The most significant consequences include possible changes to traffic flows during the transitional phase of the construction site, travel times that theoretically should decrease once the work is completed, and construction phases that could create temporary congestion and significant delays. In addition, the impact on commuting costs is considerable: gasoline consumed, car wear and tear, and time lost in queues have a direct effect on the cross-border commuter's monthly budget.
### Scenario: Before vs After Boosting
The current state sees congestion to be expected in the morning (7-9 AM) and evening (17-19 PM) rush hour, with waiting times at the Chiasso crossing point that can be significantly extended during the summer months. Commuting costs also remain high due to fuel consumption linked to reduced speed and frequent acceleration.
After the completion of the upgrade (expected scenario), traffic should move more smoothly, travel times decrease, and fuel consumption reduce per capita. However, the expectation of temporary congestion during construction work is realistic, probably lasting months depending on the scale of the project.
